ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROCEDURE ON INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government is prepared to fulfil its commitment to place a bill relating to hate propaganda on the order paper this week. However, I understand that there is no objection to this commitment being fulfilled by having the measure introduced in the other place early next week where it will be proceeded with forthwith. I am also informed that there will be a proposal to refer the measure to a joint committee of this house and the other place.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROCEDURE ON INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the announcement made by the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) is a welcome one. We must preserve and maintain democratic principles within our country, principles without which freedom would no longer exist.
Liberty is not licence. Too many have taken advantage of their belief that it is,-to undermine and destroy by direct attack, imputation, defamation and the like, the reputation of people in a group. I think it is a very good idea to have the study of this bill begun in the other place so that the fullest use may be made of that place. At the same time, through the joint committee of the two houses we will be able to bring about legislation which, while protecting the people of any one race from dangerous propaganda, will at the same time maintain a basic principle, namely the right of freedom of speech.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROCEDURE ON INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party I greet with pleasure the announcement that this legislation will be placed on the order paper, and if it is likely to be proceeded with more expeditiously in the other place, then we have no objection. speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, at the close of my remarks last night a discussion had arisen between myself and the leader of the N.D.P. concerning price reductions consequent upon the looping of the Trans-Canada pipe line through the United States. The hon. member asked me to substantiate my figures, and this I will do in a moment.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: What is the source of this list?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is the kind of thing one would normally read in the course of a speech. We agree to table documents from official sources, but if this is just part of the hon. member's speech he should take the time to read the list.

Mr. Chairman, I would think that if a list of persons opposing that application is going to be filed, then certainly at the same time there ought to be filed a list of the persons who are supporting the application, so that hon. members may have full information.

Mr. Chairman, apparently there is not unanimous agreement. It is not that serious, so I will just read some of the names and let the hon. member for Burna-by-Coquitlam measure who his allies are in this fight of his.

Those who are opposing the efforts of this Canadian company to move western Canadian gas into eastern Canadian markets include the Consumers Power Company of Michigan, the United States coal industry, the Independent Petroleum Association of America, four or five companies from Iowa, Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line Company (Trunk Line), the State of Texas, and the Texas Railroad commission. There are a lot of others who do not want to see this market in Ontario and Quebec get into the hands of western Canadian producers but want to move back into it themselves, just as they wanted to do some years ago. The full list can be obtained by reading the federal power commission reports.
During the next election, Mr. Chairman, when I go to public meetings attended by the N.D.P. I can just visualize them singing "The Yellow Rose of Texas"-instead of our national anthem, because in this particular fight they are on the side of the Texas buccaneers.

And what did you do for the
Texas buccaneers?

Our record in this matter is clear. We are the ones who set up the national energy royal commission and the National Energy Board, which has the responsibility of protecting Canadian interests. It is a court of record, and this document surely indicates how ambitious they are in protecting the Canadian interests, to the extent-
To the extent that we have to wait for the report of the United States energy board.

-to the extent that every member of the N.D.P. keeps interrupting every remark I make. I know how senstive people are when they know they are on the wrong side of an issue. I never thought the day would come when the members of the N.D.P. would be on the side of the big boys in Texas.
Mr. Chairman, the leader of the New Democratic Party asked whether I could substantiate the statement I made that I thought the price reduction consequent upon the looping through the United States would be in the neighbourhood of 10 to 15 per cent. The Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, under the National Energy Board Act, is a common carrier and has to deal with 11 different zones. I am going to take one zone as one example. I will take the example of the zone around the Sarnia area. You could call it, based on the

central point of that area, the storage wells at Dawn. I am using the figures on file with the National Energy Board which are available if anyone wishes to see them. Taking the figures of the National Energy Board, for the first three year period the price at Dawn, the storage wells near Sarnia, is 43 cents per
1,000	cubic feet. After three years the price per 1,000 cubic feet will be 45 cents. This is under the northern line route. Conditional on the new looping line being built through the United States the price will range from 39.15 cents-

speechtext: Order. I must interrupt the hon. member to advise him that the time allotted to him has expired.

I was stating that the new contracts, conditionally on the line being built, will range from 39.15 cents to 40.85 cents per 1,000 cubic feet. The mean average of those two prices is 40 cents, and I will call the new price conditional on the new line 40 cents per 1,000 cubic feet. Compared to the previous price this is a difference of 5 cents per 1,000 cubic feet for gas on a firm basis. Then there is an interruptible price of 36 cents m.c.f. In these industrial areas of southwestern Ontario this is very vital because the consumption of much of this gas is on an uninterruptible basis. Let us assume the average price in this zone is 38 cents which is half way between 36 cents and 40 cents. Therefore, on the basis of the cost factor for this one zone we can see that the wholesale price will be down, on the average, about 5 to 7 cents a thousand.
This means that the manufacturers in the whole area served by Union Gas have an opportunity to have reduced prices within this range, and it also means that those who heat their homes in this area would have an opportunity for reduced prices within this range. Under the National Energy Board Act the National Energy Board is required to see that every other zone is not discriminated against. So, these prices will apply back through the whole system, to Toronto, to London, to Sudbury, to the lakehead, to Kenora, to Manitoba and to Saskatchewan. This provision results from the application of the common carrier principle. These figures I
Interim Supply
have quoted would indicate that if you applied the same price reduction to the new line there would be a decrease in cost of 12J per cent, using 40 cents as the base. If you take the 7 cents, there is a 16 i per cent reduction.

May I ask the hon. member a question. Has his attention been drawn to page 9386 of Hansard where the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stated that in respect of any contracts which already have been in operation in northern Ontario, there is an average reduction of 3 cents.

This is exactly what I am saying. Under the National Energy Board Act, if there is any reduction in any zone served by this common carrier, the energy board is required to see that the reduction is backed up along the line. It is only natural that the price will back up in varying degrees almost to Saskatchewan. I am simply saying that the figure I quoted for the Dawn area will affect tne people around Windsor and around Toronto where the greatest reduction will take place, but that some reduction will also flow to the people in northern Ontario immediately. I think I have answered the question of the leader of the New Democratic Party. In other words, there is going to be a wholesale price reduction of, say, 10 to 15 per cent depending on the base figure. If we do not build the south loop and cannot supply the gas to southwestern Ontario and to the Hamilton-Toronto area, then these companies there will have no other source of supply except the United States, because this northern line cannot be built in 1967 when the gas is needed. Once new contracts are signed with the United States pipe lines for three or five years, then we are hooked to those contracts. The Americans will be back into our market. Our consumers will have to pay a higher price, because there is a 3 cent tariff on 1,000 cubic feet. This hits right at the Canadian domestic user.
This strikes also at the Canadian manufacturing companies who are in mortal competition for survival with the American competitors. Our price will be forced higher than the prices of the United States competitors. I simply say that, to me, this is not Canadi-anism. If we take the economic and sensible approach, that gas price will go down 10 or 15 per cent and we will be below the United States manufacturing cost. Then, our industries would have what they always have been fighting for, lower costs. This is the exercise

November 3, 1965
Interim Supply
that we in western Canada have been carrying on for nearly 10 years. In the west we have subsidized the consumers of gas in Ontario and Quebec to build up a market. We are still going to subsidize them under these new prices. We are doing it in the hope that we can give the carriers a chance to compete in the markets with their big competitors in the United States. The F.P.C. protects their people. Why should the Canadian government be the one that rides on the backs of the Canadian companies? This Canadian company is not perfect. In my judgment, in many ways, the company has been very stupid in its behavior, but it is the only true Canadian company we have; it is 92 per cent owned by Canadians now. We had to buy back the shares the hard way.
I am saying simply that I am not against opportunities for employment for those in Windsor, London, Waterloo, Hamilton, Toronto, Oshawa, Ottawa and Montreal. I am not against the nickel workers in Sudbury or the steel workers in Sault Ste. Marie.
Now I should like to put on the record the arguments, pro and con, concerning the pipe line. The arguments against building the loop through the United States are easy to explain. First, it is argued that the line should be in Canada because of the tremendous value of the construction work to the hard pressed people of northern Ontario. The construction work on the pipe line from 1956 on was a great boon to the part time workers of northern Ontario who exist through seasonal employment in the logging industry, seasonal work in the mines, and so on. The question is whether the construction should start now or in three years from now. As a matter of fact, I do not think it is any secret that the second line would have to be built anyway because the demand is growing very fast.
The second argument is that certain of the municipalities in the thinly populated areas of northern Ontario rely principally on the assessments in respect of the pipe line to pay their municipal expenses. I do not blame those councillors and reeves for demanding that the line start in 1967 rather than in 1970. I can see their point. I was born and raised there, and I know the desperate task they have to keep going.
That, however, does not meet the real question. The real problem is to decide what is best for the people in all parts of Canada. It is clear now that if we build the Southern loop next year we can supply gas more cheaply to the people in the north.

[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
We must get this gas out to the industries. The pulp mills want gas now and the mining: companies want gas now. This gas can be given to them now only if we agree to this loop to the south. We cannot give it to them immediately if we wait three years for this line to the north to be built.
Let me go on to the next argument, and this one has not really been raised in this house. One of the real fears we have, as Conservatives, is that as a result of building this line through the United States we may lose control of this gas. I well remember what happened in 1942 when the United States finally found out there was a war going on and joined in. They cut off the electricity entering Canada and forced Ontario industries to go into a "brown-out." I recall the campaign of that great Conservative leader of the province, George Drew, who wanted hydro development in Ontario so the province would never again suffer a similar brown-out because a foreign country cut off a source of energy.
Because of that fact, I believe this parliament has a right to discuss this matter of control. Under the contract with this Great Lakes company not only does the Canadian company hold 50 per cent of the shares, it has a management agreement under which it controls management. If the F.P.C. should use the power given to it to cut off the flow of gas coming into Canada, it would not mean the same thing as the cutting off of energy meant in 1942, because in this case we put the energy in at the one end and we could simply cut it off there. In that even, the United States would not be cutting off anything.
The greatest argument against United States interference with the flow is a simple one. This year hundreds of millions of cubic feet of gas will flow from Alberta and British Columbia into California and seven northern states. Would the F.P.C. cut off 170 million odd cubic feet of gas going into the market area of Michigan and Wisconsin at the risk of losing hundreds of millions of cubic feet flowing into California and those northern states? It would not be sensible to think that the United States would do that. That country is rapidly becoming a deficit country in resources and energy. It surely will not fool around with that type of thing. I suggest that the question of control can never be finally answered because we do not know what the United States might do. However the common
-November 3, 1966

sense of the situation suggests that that type of interference is over.
In the original contracts, 90 per cent of this gas was to come through to eastern Canada and 10 per cent was to be dropped off in the west. I was not worried at that time because I knew about the tremendous volume that was going from Alberta and British Columbia to California and the northwestern states. Everything was in balance. We are no longer dependent. We have a main line through the north and in three years we will start the construction of a second main line or the "twinning" in the north. This southern looping arrangement will take advantage of the economics of having storage facilities as well as volume flow.
I think I have dealt with these arguments fairly. I now wish to present another argument which has been discussed. All parties were for the northern route in 1954 and again in 1956. We won that battle. We succeeded in getting a line built through the north. As a result of the passing of the National Energy Board Act in 1959 we put control under a tough-minded board.
My only criticism of the actions of that board is that it failed to properly forecast future markets, and warn us of the danger that we would not have enough gas to meet the demands. Apparently it did not require the company to carry out its obligations. The board could have watched the actions of this company more closely.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I interrupt the hon. member for a moment to say that the National Energy Board maintains that it can prove it anticipated the developing need for gas and informed the company.
It should have started this twinning in northern Ontario three years ago.

All I can say is that if the energy board informed the company, it was lax in not telling the government that the company was not carrying out its obligations.
I have no brief for this company because I feel it should have known ahead of time of this anticipated demand and taken action to ensure we would not be in this position of having to adopt a crash program. I do not think things of this kind should be rushed.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member wants to remind this house that the company had a certain amount of difficulty in the United States before putting this project into being.
Interim Supply

I have been pretty hard on the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company, but, I know the whole situation was awkward. I know the company is having a great deal of difficulty, because of the big Texas giants, in obtaining this market. The overall picture is that there are southern and central United States gas fields. We have gas fields in British Columbia and Alberta. Both these interests are fighting for the same market. We are fighting American interests, for this eastern market, and the government has to make sure that our best interests are protected. I simply point out that the National Energy Board has been particularly tough in favour of our interests. I am glad to say that we have some guarantee that our public interests are being protected.
Let me refer to arguments for the southern loop. I do not think there is any reason why we, as Canadians, cannot today look at the situation from the point of view of Canada's interests. The Trans-Canada Pipe Lines company is now a Canadian company, being 92 per cent owned by Canadians. As the Borden royal commission pointed out in volume I of its report, Canadian interests bought out United States interests in this company. It is now a Canadian company and we must support it, as miserable as we may think it is.
Another argument for the southern loop is that it would be cheaper and would provide cheaper gas in eastern Canadian centres to the extent of 10 per cent to 15 per cent. It would also be quicker to build in that we could get gas to storage in less than a year as compared to a minimum of three years by the northern route.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
I hope I am not abusing the committee's time by answering these questions.

When the hon. member refers to the speed and economy of the southern line, is he talking about building a line in the south as compared to building a new line across the north, or twinning the present line across the north?

I know there must be a second line through the north. What I am saying is that the company was not confident enough about future needs to build a bigger line at the beginning. The line in the north should have been much bigger. In the meantime we have built up a gas market and we

November 3, 1968
Interim Supply
do not want United States encroachment. The present emergency must be met now. The arguments for the southern route are that it can be built quicker and cheaper. To get lower costs there are two basic, fundamental principles that must be remembered; volume and load factor. Lower cost will enable us to put gas into our industrial areas and reduce the cost of gas in the north. We will then be able to compete efficiently with our United States competitors.
If we can do this we will create more jobs and have a trade advantage over the United States. We will also help the domestic home owner. Another reason in favour of the southern route is that we can move quickly and stop United States penetration into Canadian markets. Seventy per cent of our total Canadian energy market lies between Windsor and Quebec. This market is of great value to the interests in Texas as well as those in Alberta. We must support the Canadian interests in serving this market.
The western Canadian interests in Alberta subsidized the creation of this market over a period of ten years, and they are prepared to continue this subsidization. However, they want in return an opportunity to eventually get a fair price for their products.
Another reason for supporting the southern route is that it will make gas available in the north immediately and that area is desperate for gas because of the growth in the Timmins, Cochrane and western Quebec areas where there are pulp mills and mining industries. These demands are far greater than anyone might have expected.
The only way we can serve this rapidly growing area is by getting gas into the southern areas, which is the premium market, and thereby free more gas from the northern line. If the southern loop is built, one must not forget that gas will then be three cents cheaper in the north, and this surely is of some advantage to the mining industry and the pulp mills.
Another reason for supporting the southern route is that, for the first time, gas will be made available to the city of Sault Ste. Marie which is one of our great steel cities. It has not been served by gas, but this will give it a chance to get Canadian gas at an advantageous price, having in mind the provisions of the National Energy Board Act guaranteeing non discrimination in prices. In this way they would get cheaper gas than areas further toward the centres of Ontario and Quebec.

[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Fifth, the southern loop would make possible and more feasible the installation of pipe lines from Montreal to Quebec city. I know this question has been discussed for many years, but with the present price structure it is not feasible or economical to build a line around the south shore of the city of Montreal to Three Rivers and Quebec and one line around the north shore. However, this new price structure would make it possible for the government of Quebec to deal with Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, or whatever distributing agency is set up, on the basis of a price which would give them a chance of being in a profit position in the next few years.
In this respect, I make a special plea for the people who live on the north and south shores of the St. Lawrence beyond Montreal. They have a right to the development that will come from the economic and efficient use of natural gas. Not only would the cost of heating their homes be reduced but the provision of gas would benefit the light industries in these areas, which would mean so much in raising the standard of living of their people. This is something we could do that would help our country to develop more equally. I enter a strong plea for the people between the cities of Montreal and Quebec.
Sixth, it would help find a market for western producers. As was illustrated in the speech of the hon. member for Bow River, our supplies have escalated, and I know they will continue to escalate. The ratio of gas exported to our capacity to produce is growing smaller all the time. We would like to expand our markets and keep our exploration going. I will not say any more about that aspect of the matter, Mr. Chairman. We hope that if this market builds up we in the west will some day obtain a fair price for our gas.
The seventh point-and this is the most important one-is that this loop would fit in with a long range energy policy for Canada. A good energy policy for Canada should have these three principles: First, the supply of energy in Canada should be available to Canadians first for as long ahead as we can see. Whether we look to the year 2000 or 2100, the first principle should be security of supply for any type of development that occurs in the next 100 or 150 years. We can make this possible. The second principle of energy policy should be that our Canadian energy should be cheaper in Canada than it is to our competitors anywhere in North
November 3, 1966

America. We have so much of this energy, but if we are not careful it will pour south and not only will Canadians not have a chance to get it back but if some is fed back from the United States we will pay more for it.
So the first two principles are, availability of gas to Canadians first and, second, cheaper gas for Canadians. The third principle has not been put into effect as yet, but I hope that one day we will have in power a government that will put it into effect. We should utilize the east-west connections. This would provide the mechanisms cheaper gas and cheaper energy. We should use the mechanisms we have set up to bargain with the United States in order to obtain a higher return for all the energy exported from this country. In this connection, we should use our bargaining power as a Federal government and not leave the bargaining to the provinces or the private Canadian companies producing energy. I believe the Canadian interest demands that we take a national interest in bargaining for our energy, and the National Energy Board Act provides the machinery whereby we can carry out this bargaining.
The three principles are clear. First, availability of supply to Canadians first and, second, always at a reduced cost to Canadians. Then, we should use the bargaining power of the nation to make sure that our competitors always pay more for energy if we export it. This principle applies not only to gas. We have the main line for gas in Canada now. We eventually must have a main line for oil in Canada. We have to make our deal with Venezuela, not with the Texas Railroad Commission which now determines who buys and sells in what markets around the world. We acted independently in 1960-61 with regard to a national oil policy. It is time to review that policy, not in the sense of selfish nationalism but to make sure that Canadians not only gain access to their own product but obtain it at a cheaper rate than our competitors pay. When we bargain with another country we must bargain from strength.
Another form of energy which we must safeguard is electricity. In September, 1959, the then Prime Minister announced that we had to work toward a national transmission power grid. I believe this announcement was made at Kitimat. This is what our party has done in this field. Oil, gas and electricity are forms of energy. There must be east-west
Interim Supply
connections for them. Only then can we develop the lines to the north and south safely. The east-west connections must be developed in order that Canadians may gain access to these forms of energy first, at a lower cost, and in order to provide us with bargaining power. In the past the bargaining is usually carried out by the provinces or those companies which own the energy.
I place these principles in regard to a long range energy policy before the committee, because if I have any quarrel with the minister it is that he has not yet had time or has not yet seen fit to put before the nation his concept of a national energy policy. We should like to know where we are going in this connection. We should like to know the thinking of the National Energy Board and the government in reference to these resources, so that parliament may deal with these questions.
I am grateful to the committee for extending my time. I should now like to place before the committee a brief summary of my points. We have today the great gas areas in the central and southern United States. We have the great gas provinces of Alberta, British Columbia and the Territories. These areas are engaged in a struggle, through the private companies, to gain control of the markets in California and the central and eastern part of this continent. We know this is a struggle between powerful giants. There are many such giants in the United States -Tennessee, Panhandle, El Paso, among others. In Canada we have really only one giant selling eastward, namely, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. Regardless of what we think about this company, we have no choice as Canadians but to back the Canadian giant in this fight, particularly for a Canadian market. That is the first thing I say in summary, Mr. Chairman.
Those in the east should know that we in the west have gladly subsidized the building up of markets in Ontario by accepting a much lower price for sales into this province than we could obtain by selling to the south. We have done this willingly as Canadians, and are prepared to continue doing it; but we would like to see this problem handled economically. We know that if we could get the price down in Ontario and Quebec, the volume of sales would climb dramatically. This would mean a lower cost per unit. Then perhaps we could lower the price still more and obtain a better return in the west at the same time.

November 3, 1966
Interim Supply
I know that this whole program is ordinarily left to the National Energy Board. Last March I rose in the house in chagrin because this Canadian company, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, endeavouring to bring Canadian gas into Canada, had to have its application approved by the F.P.C. I know that under United States law due process of law must be applied to every pipe line moving through the United States. But this was Canadian gas which would be going to Canada. I thought, as the Borden commission recommended, our government should have gone to the United States government and said: This is really a matter of border accommodation. Let one of our representatives on the National Energy Board sit with your F.P.C. to watch the proceedings; and when we have an application for one of your operations to come through our country, you can send one of your people up here to watch our operations. But do not make this Canadian company go through the tremendously expensive and detailed battle with these powerful American giants, which battle will go on for months, when we desperately need this gas in eastern Canada.
The Minister of Finance did not see any loss of Canadian sovereignty. I can understand that when we move gas from one part of Canada to another, and as a courtesy also move it through the United States, we have to go through the long procedure which the United States authorities require, naturally, to protect their interests. But this was a Canadian matter. If the United States authority objected to 10 per cent of the gas being dropped off, it could have been cut to 5 per cent of whatever amount was needed to satisfy the people in the area through which the line ran.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
They have no moral right to interfere with Canadian business. Technically this is not an infringement of our sovereignty but in a moral sense and in a neighbourly sense it is. On this issue I do not blame those members for bringing briefs here from their counsellors in the north who want construction to start this year instead of in 1970. I do not blame them for backing up that stand, but I ask them to look at those with whom they are standing. I would not want to be caught standing with the opponents of Canada on this issue.
I would also ask them to look at the price of this project. Surely this is a serious consideration in view of the high prices that now

prevail. People are paying high prices to keep their families in the cities and it is our responsibility to make it possible for them to do so. This applies to everyone, to the working people, to clerks in stores and to everyone else. Whenever Canada is pressured by high prices, as it is today, surely we should support every move to reduce those prices.
Mr. Chairman, I have a suspicion that this whole row in Canada did not develop in support of the Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line's opposition to this movement of gas to eastern from western Canada. I know that Panhandle wishes to return to our market in a big way.
I think the whole battle started because a group of politicians were fighting over one seat, and they thought they could have the local battle moved right into the federal parliament. But surely the interests of Canadians are more important than the fortunes of the Liberal or NDP parties in some northern constituency. Everybody knows the seat to which I am referring.
I think the government has been weak. I do not think the government's first statement was thought out very well and whoever wrote it deserves the criticism it received from the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. The minister will never be able to explain it away.
But he did.

Mr. Chairman, I do not even want to start discussing this subject. I believe in peace, order and good government. I have exposed the government's shallowness of judgement. I thought it had enough criticism from the leader of the New Democratic Party. When he began to question the minister the latter must have realized he had no answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: You quoted it yourself.

In September I listed the eight points on which I thought the government should change its mind. I congratulate the government for changing its mind, but I do not congratulate it for being so weak. Although it realized what the issue was, it got us into this whole mess. This type of decision should be under the jurisdiction of the National Energy Board because political pressures should not be allowed to decide the future of this country.
Mr. Chairman, I have spoken with some feeling on this subject because I am convinced that somebody should speak for the consumers of Ontario and Quebec. I am speaking also for the many Canadians who
November 3, 1966

want jobs in the future. Once we achieve a lower price structure for energy than the one in the United States we will have a competitive advantage, and it will mean more jobs for Canadians. Above all I think I am speaking for the people of northern Ontario who, first of all, want cheaper gas and more gas now. They do not really want to wait three years for gas and pay higher prices now and later. I am a Canadian first and foremost. I have tried to bring out all of the facts. I hope that, on that basis, this southern loop will be supported.

May I ask the hon. member a question before he sits down? He has made a number of prophecies regarding gas being brought in by the northern line and how long it will take. Would he like to make a prophecy as to when he thinks a decision will be made by the national energy board in the United States on whether or not they can sell gas to the United States through that line?

Mr. Chairman, I think that is the crux of the reason I am pleading so hard. The F.P.C. has had this application before them for over a year. Now it is being held in abeyance because the opposition to this scheme sees this debate in the house as a chance to bring in arguments which would hold it up for another year. If we do not have that gas in the next few months, United States pipe lines can move right in tomorrow and supply the market. You cannot blame them for trying to out-deal us. This must be clear to the F.P.C. Surely, if the government went to the F.P.C. and said: "Would you please expedite this matter", they would throw out these extraneous applications which were brought in by the competitors to this route and come to some conclusion. I would not even begin to say when a United States court of law will hand down a decision. I would hope they could do it by December or January of this year.
We could build a line in the north much sooner. It would take much longer to get a decision from the United States.

Mr. Chairman, if I
may, I would like to deal with a matter entirely different from what has been discussed during examination of interim supply. In fact, I would like to call the attention of the house to the matter of railway crossings 23033-600
Interim Supply
which is daily becoming a matter of national urgency, in view of the numerous tragedies which occur everywhere and the terrible calamities which have struck our people, particularly during the last few weeks.
There is no doubt that highway safety, as a whole, is a major concern of all authorities, of all specialized organizations in that field, and the danger that railway crossings represent is a distressing and alarming part of the highway safety problem.
Over the past 15 years, that is between 1950 and 1965 inclusive, car-train collisions at railway crossings have been responsible for 2,694 deaths in Canada. In the province of Quebec, more specifically, there were 617 fatal accidents due to collisions between trains and motor vehicles.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
This percentage may not be very large compared to the countless tragedies taking place on our highways, but it is nevertheless quite an alarming figure which calls for special attention, I am sure, from the authorities concerned. That is the reason for my short intervention this afternoon, Mr. Chairman.
I would like to outline this alarming situation by taking my stand on undeniable figures, and not by complaining, which is so characteristic of the province of Quebec. There is one thing which strikes one's imagination when one reads the annual report of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada for the year ending on December 31, 1965. We can see-and I do not want to be accused of being a secessionist, or one who insists persistently on Quebec's rights-that figures are eloquent and prompt us to say categorically that Quebec has not been given its fair share of the grade crossing fund.
Mr. Chairman, as a basic remark, may I point out that safety signals placed at grade crossings are installed under the grade crossing fund, to which the Board of Transport Commissioners, or the federal government, as you wish, contributes 80 per cent. As can be seen on page 37 of the board's report, Ontario received since 1909, when the grade crossing fund was set up, the amount of $54,195,379.99. On the other hand, the province of Quebec received $15,506,565.96. Ontario and Quebec account for 34.5 per cent and 28.9 per cent respectively of the total population of Canada. There is a discrimination there, if we consider that Ontario received $54 million and more since 1909 while Quebec received $15,506,000 only.

November 3, 1966
Interim, Supply
We are justified in concluding from these figures that the province of Quebec did not get its fair share. There is an explanation to this. When it is necessary to provide protection at grade crossings, the Board of Transport Commissioners, through the grade crossing fund, pays 80 per cent of the cost, whether it be for signal fights, an underpass, an overpass or some other protective device. On the other hand, the railways must contribute 15 per cent and the local authorities, either the province or the municipality must contribute 5 per cent of the cost in the case of signal fights, and 7.5 per cent in the case of an underpass or an overpass. The maximum amount the Board of Transport Commissioners is allowed to spend for the construction of an underpass and an overpass is $500,000. When it comes to building very expensive works, which sometimes result in expenditures of more than $1 or $2 millions, it happens that the municipalities cannot afford to spend more than a definite amount and that is the reason why those municipalities which cannot afford to spend the necessary amount to meet the required condition of 5 or 7.5 per cent do not ask for adequate protection. Therefore, no request having been made, the railway grade crossing fund is not called upon to contribute to the cost of the facilities which should be built but are not because the municipality, the local authority concerned, is too poor to assume its share of the necessary contribution under the present act.
Therefore, concluding that Quebec did not get its fair share, an improvement is called for, an amendment to the act is needed. At the present time, three authorities are called upon to contribute: the railways, the provincial or municipal authorities and the Board of Transport Commissioners.
When a matter as urgent as the security and life of others is concerned, an administrative simplification is needed, on the one hand, and a single authority should be called upon, if not to decide unilaterally, at least to contribute as a single source of income in the expenditures resulting from the construction of the said protective system. That is the problem which arises and that is the reason why Quebec did not get its fair share from the railway grade crossing fund.
I therefore, call upon the authorities to study that very urgent problem and thus prevent those mass killings which we have to deplore so often. I am thinking in particular of the frightening tragedy at Dorion; I am

also thinking of the tragedy at Val Alain, in the riding of Lotbiniere; I have in mind also the recent tragedy which happened at Mont-magny the day before yesterday when a train was going at the allowed speed of 50 or 60 miles an hour in a city where there are no signal lights. One has the right then to sound the alarm and say that there is a very urgent problem which must be solved as efficiently as possible.
There are some possible solutions; a great number of solutions have been proposed. I would like to mention, for instance, what some safety organizations recommended, that is the compulsory stopping of all cars at level crossing where there are signs only. There are several level crossings where there are signs and, to prove it, I am using the statistics for 1965. In the province of Quebec, out of 33 deaths due to accidents at level crossings, 23 took place where there were signs only. That is certainly conclusive evidence that mere signs do not give adequate protection.
In the province of Quebec, in 1965, out of 153 people injured in accidents at level crossings, 85 were injured where there were signs only. Signs are not an adequate protection. They just say "Railway Crossings", and quite often drivers see them but do not stop. For the information of those who complain that French signs are put up on federal buildings in the Catholic and French speaking province of Quebec, I point out that only the words "Railway Crossing" appear. And not a single French Canadian member has complained fanatically, as some hon. members opposite have done because a sign saying: "Edifice Federal" was put up on a federal building in a supposedly bilingual country. There is no fanaticism on the government side, Mr. Chairman; we want to respect both languages.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
We are proud, we are pleased that English is used in Quebec. But we should also like to see some French in the English speaking provinces, so that the bilingual character of our country might be respected.
Enough of that digression, and back to the heart of the matter. I was enumerating the main solutions which have been suggested. There should be a compulsory stop for all automobiles and a warning signal equipped with a light, in such a way that drivers would have to stop and look.
Second, and I insist on this point, all road signs should be removed and replaced if
November 3, 1966

possible, by warning lights. Now, installation of those lights might run into exorbitant expenses; according to the experts, this might cost $40,000, $45,000 or even $50,000.
There are 30,000 grade crossings in Canada. If the figures are accurate, Mr. Chairman, at 20,000, that is, two thirds of them, there are only signs. I have here the figures for the province of Quebec only. Total grade crossings in Quebec: 3,483; signs, 2,040, almost two thirds; flashing signals, 829; overpasses and underpasses, 448; gates, 68. That is the protection given in the province of Quebec.
Shame.

In agreement with the member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) who has always understood the problems of Quebec, I say "shame" too, Mr. Chairman. Let us, therefore, remove that cause of shame which has often resulted in such unfortunate tragedies that often make the headlines in the papers.
Another solution: a reasonable speed limit for trains. It is certainly excessive when trains, in a municipality such as Dorion or Montmagny, are authorized to travel at 50 or 60 miles per hour. A car driver travelling at such a speed in a town like Montmagny would not only be charged with dangerous driving if arrested after killing someone, but would also be charged with criminal negligence.
Railway companies have full and complete control over the railway, no matter where it is located. Trains can pass. They are above humanitarian principles, so to speak. They do not have to worry, the road is there. The trains can travel at the legal speeds of 60, 70, 80 miles per hour, and nobody will stop them.
Mr. Chairman, that is deplorable. In such a case, strict legislation is a must. There must be established a reasonable limit to force trains to slow down at those perilous places, that is grade crossings.
Another solution is to install rotary lights on locomotives. That would not be so expensive. But there is no doubt that a rotary light on a locomotive would get the driver's attention.
I would not want to appear too partial. I have had the opportunity to know a person whose proposed solution was convex mirrors. I have referred to that in the house in the past.
Interim Supply
Again, sir, this solution is not expensive. Convex mirrors gives a view in both directions, so that one can see approaching trains.
To the traffic lights, we can add the convex mirrors; to the traffic lights and the convex mirrors, we can add the rotating lights. Maximum safety is required in those places.
Coming back to what I said earlier, administrative simplification will make it possible for a single authority to decide, or at least to pay in that regard. Those are tentative solutions upon which we must insist and I believe that if only one authority paid for the installation of protection systems, Quebec could get back what it has lost since 1909, namely the amount which normally it would have received from the railway grade crossing fund.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I believe that those few solutions, which I wanted to offer in all humility, if considered in depth, since the problem is urgent, could avoid several of those tragedies.
I should also like to emphasize that the grade crossing fund provides at the present time an inadequate amount: $15 million a year. I am not speaking for Quebec only but for Canada as a whole, $15 million a year.
When one thinks of all the highway safety campaigns. Some even advocate setting up a royal inquiry on highway safety. Such inquiries are unnecessary. We already have too many at the present time. And whom do they benefit? The lawyers, in most cases, and practical solutions do not come as fast as we would like them to. I am not afraid to say so, because I know that it is true. I know that this pleases the hon. member for Ville-neuve (Mr. Caouette), I know that he would be in favour. There are some practical solutions ready made, which could be implemented. And since the railway crossing problem is part and parcel of the overall problem of highway safety, therefore let us not lose any time and consider all those solutions provided by safety organizations and let us implement them without delay. There is no need to wait for the result of inquiries. In Dorion, the inquiry will show that there was an accident with casualties. But what we want is a solution which can be applied at once. All those solutions have been clearly and expressly suggested, so that the authorities when contacted should be aware of them already.
I want to say it again, because it is beyond1 question and it has been proven in the report of the commission on transportation, since

November 3, 1966
Interim Supply
Quebec did not get its share, if we apply all the solutions offered from all sides, Quebec will be in a position to get back the moneys it did not receive and in doing so, we shall have greatly served the humanitarian cause.

Mr. Chairman, during the discussion on estimates, I wish to deal with two subjects: national defence and the recent federal-provincial conference.
Over the past few days, several speakers have referred to differences of opinion which have come about between certain officers in our armed forces and the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer).
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I,	for one, agree with the statements of the hon. Minister of National Defence and the hon. Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) in connection with the reasons for integrating our three armed services and in respect of the feelings of resentment between the hon. minister and certain officers in the armed forces.
I accept, Mr. Chairman, these statements made by persons in authority here, in this house, because I feel that governmental and popular authority should supersede our armed forces and their officers. As a matter of fact, these people must serve our population. It would be unfortunate if here, either through weakness or carelessness, we let it become an accepted fact in this country, as has been the case in a number of countries, in Latin America and in Eastern countries, for instance, where the army and its superior officers constantly stood up to the government in office and took advantage of specific crises, economic or otherwise, to take over administrative authority.
Well, I commend the hon. minister's firmness in this matter, and I wish to assure him he has my support. On the other hand, I wish to remind him that the government should consider reducing even more the national defence budget. In the estimates brought before the house by the hon. Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp) some time in March 1966, again we see that the budget for national defence is too high considering the size of our country.
Indeed, out of every dollar spent on administration, 19 cents go towards national defence, 14 cents towards the public debt charges-it is fantastic that we should have to pay 14 cents out of every dollar for the national debt-and only 6 cents to the

provincial and municipal administrations. Glancing at the budgets for national defence throughout the years, we see that, in 1938, it amounted to $34,432,023; in 1941, during the war, to $1,339,674,152; in 1965, to $1,535,634,697; in 1966, to $1,561,385,193; and, for 1967, climbing even higher, it reaches $1,572,690,000.
We note that, in peacetime, our expenditures for national defence increase constantly and that they even exceed those for 1941 when Canada was at war.
I understand that the minister pointed out in his presentation that he had reduced by
23,000	the number of personnel in the armed services, thus saving the country $150 million. But what the minister saves in a way, he does not save for the treasury but spends in his department, in other areas, for equipment.
Canada becomes involved in all sorts of military undertakings. The government buys airplanes or experiments with some war devices. Now, these often prove unsuccessful and lead to waste. More often than not, when this equipment is fully developed, it is already outdated by newer material which is more advanced and more precise. The government should take a second look at its policy respecting national defence. It ought to cut public expenditures in order to use those savings for the well-being of the Canadian people.
Mr. Chairman, there is no reason to spend so much money in peace time: $1,572,690,000 in 1967. I believe that we should reduce the present budget of the Department of National Defence by at least 40 per cent, while taking into account the real contribution of Canada on the world scene.
I know very well that Canada is a member of various international organizations, and that it is the neighbour of the United States, but thousands of Canadians are of the opinion that we should limit our activities outside Canada, especially in the military field.
I cannot accept the statement made by the Associate Minister of National Defence, which is to be found on page 9396 of this session's official report, in which he pointed out with emphasis that we had armed forces in Cyprus, the Negev desert, West Germany and that we were defending Canada by having Canadian forces in those countries. Personally, I am not convinced that by moving our Canadian forces in such numbers outside Canada, we are defending Canada directly. On the contrary, if we are there, it is because of questionable ties.
November 3, 1966

Canada directly. On the contrary, if we are there, it is because of questionable political ties.
I would appreciate it very much if the hon. minister and the government considered, from now on, reducing our expenditures abroad. All the money we could thus save. With a billion-dollar budget, Canada would be able to meet all its obligations according to its capacities and ear-mark such savings for high-priority problems concerning the whole Canadian people. Such high-priority problems are related to poverty in Canada, to the economic and political fields. Numerous investigations for some years have shown that millions of Canadian people are living in poverty.
Now, the government should save more money by reducing the expenditures of the Department of National Defence. In spite of all requests made by several hon. members, the government still refuses to increase old age pensions immediately to $100 at least, without a means test. Mr. Chairman, this is essential and meets the needs of our older citizens, and it is also a patriotic gesture towards them.
The money saved could be well spent on relieving the poverty of many Canadian families, for example by increasing family allowances and veterans allowances.
It is all very well for the Department of National Defence to undertake, often impulsively, so many fruitless experiments with military equipment, but it should save money in order to provide better pensions for those who fought in the last world war and came back disabled. These Canadians deserve better treatment from the Canadian government.
With these savings, I think that the Canadian government could fulfil its responsibilities by helping all these people more. Charity begins at home. Charity properly practised should first consist in raising the standard of living of the people of this country.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Another high-priority problem, which the government should endeavour to settle and for which could profitably be used the savings made with respect to national defence, is related to the economic field: price increase and inflation. We do not have enough time this afternoon to dwell on those questions, but those are the facts. We see more and more in the main Canadian cities, thousands of housewives grouped together to protest against supermarkets, and this is the most
Interim Supply
direct way of protesting against price increases. And what is the government doing about this alarming problem? It barely admits that there is some inflation. The government sees that productivity in Canada is not increasing as fast as prices, since price increases exceed by 3 per cent our productivity increase. Now, a vast and prosperous country like Canada should urge our government to increase our productivity and, in my opinion, the best way to do it would be to prompt our industries to hand over more money to the provinces so as to enable them, within their respective territory, to provide assistance at every economic and industrial level and thus spend more money in the field of scientific and industrial research.
Another high-priority problem is to be found in the political field, and I wish to refer briefly to the recent federal-provincial conference. As I said earlier, in the latest estimates of March 1966, only 6 cents out of every dollar have been allocated to the payments made to the provinces; following the slight increase offered to the provinces during the last federal-provincial conference, Ottawa's contribution to the provinces will perhaps reach 7 or 7.5 cents for every dollar spent. That is still not enough. The last federal-provincial conference showed that the provinces and municipalities will be increasingly short of money and that in 1972, their deficit will reach almost $2 billion, whereas the federal government will probably have a $1 billion surplus.
In spite of all those findings and figures divulged to the ministers of the crown by the tax structure committee, in spite of all the pressing and increasing needs of provinces and municipalities, the present government missed the finest opportunity to create harmony in the country, to be fair and to share out equitably the fiscal fields in Canada, so as to enable all institutions which will be faced with more problems within the next five years, to meet their obligations.
At this federal-provincial conference, the spirit and the letter of the 1867 constitution continued to be repudiated as regards adult education, assistance to higher education, research, culture, tax sharing, on the basis of needs, and the obligations of the provinces. Ottawa ignores the real principles of federalism, in its federal-provincial conferences. This government refuses to create a parliamentary committee to modernize our Canadian constitution in accordance with the problems of

November 3, 1966
Interim Supply
1966-67. This government simply holds federal provincial conferences from time to time where it takes autocratic attitudes which are highly inconsistent with the application of true federalism.
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, the principles of true federalism include the following ten features: independent equal governments; a clear-cut division of taxation powers; a balance between the different governments; the supremacy of the constitution; the objectivity of the courts; the expression of freedom and security; a pluralist concept of the common good; the bringing together of ethnic groups rather than their unification; residual powers left to the provinces and a Senate to which provinces could also appoint members.
Those are the true principles of federalism. This government refuses to tackle the issue, to enable us, as legislators, in this house and in the other place, to define the Canadian responsibilities according to the principles of a true federalism.
On the contrary, even at that last federal-provincial conference, the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) maintained an unbending attitude. He could see, as well as all the Canadian people, as all the provincial ministers, the increasing provincial and municipal responsibilities and needs and in spte of such bare facts, the Minister of Finance adopted an utterly miserly and adamant position; thereby, and with the support of his government, he has increased tensions in Canada, which prevent the achievement of national understanding and unity in the full sense of the word.
Even though the ministers of this government may talk sometimes, with respect to that federal-provincial conference, about a new federalism, a democratic federalism, as the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Sauve) called it, I say that such a term is being ridiculously used and that, on the contrary, the position assumed by this government and its reluctance to try and understand the problems with which this country, the provinces and the municipalities are faced, are making of this federalism one that is not new here in Ottawa, one that I would call an autocratic federalism.
I must say I am also disappointed in the attitude of the hon. ministers in the present government who come from my province. They knew this was an excellent opportunity to assert themselves, especially in view of their number within the Liberal party; but,

once again, we witnessed silence, resignation and submissiveness. In acting like this, the hon. ministers who come from my province certainly did not fulfill the aspirations of Quebec, to which province they will have to answer at the next national election.
Even the Parliamentary Secretary to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) said this week to the Richelieu Club of Cap de la Madeleine that our province and its leaders were not politically mature and only engaged in taken struggles. This statement is indeed regrettable, Mr. Chairman. I also deplore the fact that the hon. members from the province of Quebec, because of their appointment to Ottawa, accuse the government of Quebec and its leaders, whoever they may be, of being politically immature, whereas we know that for a 100 years-and I say this without political partisanship, whether under Mercier, Gouin, Taschereau, Duplessis, Sauve, Lesage or Johnson-while the premiers have accepted the terms of the confederation pact of 1867, the leaders of the province of Quebec have always shown themselves to be politically mature and honest by adhering to the terms of the confederation pact of 1867.
And when I see the hon. members for the province of Quebec here, in this house and elsewhere, accusing the Quebec leaders of lacking in maturity, I feel that they are the ones who lack maturity, who apply themselves to acting the old dotards and quitters in the face of problems.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I remember how, in 1964, for instance, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice-Lafleche tried to explain that federal aid in the form of student loans was constitutional because the federal government was already making farm loans, when we know that, by virtue of Section 95 of the constitution, agriculture is both a federal and provincial responsibility, but that, under the same section, education, for instance, falls strictly under provincial jurisdiction.
We also had, at that time, the hon. Minister for Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin) who, at a banquet in his riding, declared that if his government introduced such a measure, he would vote against it. A measure was introduced while the hon. minister was absent from the house and he did not commit himself. We see that he has been able to climb the ladder since.
Mr. Chairman, we also have the hon. members for Mount Royal and Hochelaga (Messrs.

Trudeau and Pelletier) who seldom speak up on important matters in the house but who at numerous banquets in Toronto, Montreal and elsewhere, claim that the province of Quebec should not have a special status, although we can quote about ten sections in the Canadian constitution of 1867 which provide a special status to the province of Quebec.
For instance, as far as the appointment of judges of the superior court are concerned, it is stipulated that they must be chosen among the members of the bar of the province of Quebec. Moreover, it is also provided that the central government, with the nine English speaking provinces, can standardize all English legislation in the country while, according to a clause in the constitution, this cannot be done as far as Quebec civil laws are concerned.
Those are the criteria of the special status. But despite these constitutional provisions, we see that the Quebec members, instead of assuming their responsibilities in this house, instead of displaying political maturity, are sitting here as defeatists and renegades, as it were. I submit those are the people who do the most wrong to Canada and the province of Quebec, and I deplore that situation. I say in this house how much I would like these members to take part in the debate on such important matters, so that we may have the opportunity to reply to their learned arguments. Such opportunity is not given to us very often since they are well known for their silence.
Mr. Chairman, to conclude, I want to congratulate the member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) for having raised such an important matter this afternoon. I see that the hon. member pats himself on the back. That is real autonomy. Yes, indeed, with regard to that question of grade crossings, he was right in saying that the province of Quebec had not received its just share of this fund, and the same thing applies to many other fields.
And this is also a fact as far as the construction of railroads is concerned. The province of Quebec has never been favoured and has never received its just share because it has only 11 per cent, I believe, of Canadian railroads.
I agree with the suggestions made by the hon. member to simplify the administration so as to accelerate the elimination of grade crossings, the removal of signs and the enforcement of a speed limit. On the other

hand, I think that the public should be encouraged to be more careful.
On a recent Montreal-Sherbrooke trip, I asked the train conductor for permission to go on board the engine precisely in order to study this question of railway crossings and to see how automobile drivers behaved. And I listened to the comments of the train conductor, the engineer, the brakeman, in this regard. It is fantastic the way the public forgets about the most basic safety rules. Drivers often see the train coming, but think they have time to cross the tracks. It sometimes happens that, once on the tracks, the driver makes a wrong move or the motor fails and the car stalls, and that terrible collision occurs.
Several railway crossings are equipped with gates which block half the entrance to the railway crossing area on each side. Well, a great many drivers go around these gates just as the train is approaching the crossing.
I feel it would be advisable to urge the Canadian people to be careful, to play it safe, and not just blame the railway employees for these accidents. These people are doing a great job, but they cannot perform miracles when the train is speeding on at 50 or 60 miles per hour and they come across careless drivers such as those I described a while ago. Those drivers who carelessly attempt to cross the tracks under such circumstances are the only ones to blame.
Would the hon. member allow me to ask him a question?

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased at this time to have an opportunity to make some contribution to this debate on interim supply. Before I touch upon the main subjects with which I shall deal in my speech, let me say that it is surprising to find only one minister in this house to hear what hon. members have to say about these unquestionably important subjects and the supply situation. The government has now passed its period of grace in so far as supply is concerned and must get this motion through or face a serious difficulty. For that reason, it is amazing that those ministers who should be concerned with the subjects being discussed are not in the house at this time.
There are several other things I wish to say about this government before I refer to my main topics. This government appears to be running scared. This is apparent from the

speeches of the members on the government side in which they alluded to gallant Canadians who have served this country well, and who cannot answer for themselves in this house. It is about time the Minister of National Defence and the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, who put on a disgraceful performance last night, learned that they should not in all decency vituperate against individuals such as my very long-standing friend Admiral Brock, whom I hold in the highest regard.

I believe that in his inner heart the minister is not in accord with all aspects of the policy he has enunciated. I am sure he would not be in accord with them if he stopped to think of the damage his actions are doing to Canada, our defence forces and perhaps even to himself. I shall return a little later to the subject of the minister, because naturally I have several things to say about the present situation in the Department of National Defence.
Many times in the past three or four years people have asked me: Why doesn't the government pack it all up and leave it to the civil servants to run the country? Of course, I have replied immediately: Well, who is running the country today? The Prime Minister is a former senior civil servant, and seven or eight of this cabinet were senior civil servants. Look at the job they are doing.
To realize what sort of job they are doing, we have only to think of the pension plan, the auto agreement-there's a dilly, if ever there was one-and the medicare plan which was put before parliament recently. There are 26 ministers, of whom only six, or perhaps seven, really pull their weight. The rest appear to be nothing but a bunch of sybarites who do not seem to realize that they have a responsibility to attend to the affairs of this nation.
Shame.

means to me that you put all the service men into a pot or a dish, get them all mixed up together, just as if you put a bunch of oranges, lemons and some grapefruit together. . . to strive for peace, good will and friendship among all nations, at the same time advocating the maintenance by Canada of adequate and sufficient forces on land, sea and in the air for the defence of our country".

It goes on to say:
Our members appreciate fully the need for both good fighting equipment and well-trained fighting men. We also know from our own experience that the best equipment in the world in the hands of servicemen with low morale and with little esprit de corps cannot produce an efficient, effective fighting force. Morale and esprit de corps cannot be purchased by money alone; they must be developed and carefully nurtured.
We have been deeply concerned-
As have we all.
-at some of the public statements which have been made lately, both by those opposing and those proposing complete unification of the Canadian forces. In spite of our best efforts to understand the situation we are compelled to say that, because of the lack of authoritative, clear-cut information and explanation we find ourselves unable at this moment to form a sound judgment on the whole question.
The article goes on to say:
The Royal Canadian Legion is not interested in the partisan politics which appear to be developing in connection with this question. We are, however, deeply concerned about the question of the state and condition of our defence forces at any given time. It appears to us that sufficient thought and planning have not been given to the important questions of tradition, morale and esprit de corps or, if so, the members of Canada's forces and the public have certainly been kept in ignorance.
The Royal Canadian Legion urges your government to make clear, without further delay, the detailed plans connected with the integration, and particularly the proposed unification, of the forces so that the judgments made by Canadian organizations and citizens will be based on frank and comprehensive official information and fact, not on rumour and supposition, as seems to be largely the case at the present time.

The sub-executive committee of the Legion's Dominion Executive Council at its meeting last weekend expressed grave concern over this matter and instructed that you and your government be requested to make available the necessary information as soon as possible in the interests of the security and defence of our beloved country.
To this submission, the Prime Minister replied in a letter dated September 19 which reads as follows:
Thank you for your letter of August 26th. I appreciate your concern over the recent discussion over the unification of our armed forces. I wish to make it clear that no changes in the present constitution of the armed forces can or will be instituted until parliament has had an opportunity to debate fully such proposed changes.
To this end, it is expected that the legislation necessary to carry further the reorganization of the services will be referred to the standing committee on national defence. That ends the quotation from the Prime Minister's letter.
Charles Lynch, writing in the Ottawa Citizen yesterday, November 2, ends his article by saying:
Now, the case for calling the committee is so strong that the reflection is squarely upon Mr. Hellyer.
Read it all into the record.

The whole thing? It certainly gives the hon. member a real build-up.
I wonder how hon. members like the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, who was a navy man, and the hon. member for Saint-Antoine-Westmount, who was a noted soldier in his day, feel about the unification proposals at the present time.
