speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
In the few minutes available to me tonight, I should like to talk about resource development and the way in which our resources might best be developed in the interest of Canadians as a whole. I propose to outline a few principles which I believe we

should observe when exporting primary resources and semi-finished products to foreign countries.
I cannot resist being drawn into what I regard as a phony debate, that is, the debate between the Canadian nationalists and the continentalists. I do not think there is anyone in this house who would openly avow that he is a continentalist. We may differ in our views but I think all of us in our peculiar ways regard ourselves as Canadian nationalists, and believe we are here to promote the best interests of the country and to be as perceptive in that pursuit as we can.
My idea of a continentalist-and there are very few to be found in government circles-is one who thinks predominantly in terms of the great mass of consumers and who thinks little about the position of producers, particularly producers of raw materials. Canada will, for some time to come, be a producer of raw materials, and in this role we will have to drive the hardest possible bargain in terms of the prices for and quantity of our exports.
A good Canadian nationalist is one who, thinking over a relatively short term, five or ten years, is business-like in the best sense of the word, getting the best possible prices for his Canadian exports. He must also take a broader view; he must be statesmanlike and look into the more distant future to assess the consequences of short term arrangements and adjust them in the light of the Canadian interest in the longer term.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I have said that I believe Canadians must resist the continental approach to development. They must resist the temptation to sell both at cost and at cost plus the so-called reasonable rate of return. Instead, they must charge all that the export market will bear. They must make a handsome profit on their Canadian operations and not be content to make merely a reasonable rate of return on purely resource extractive processes.
In lots of ways Canada's natural resources are unique in quality, in cost, in extent and in location. They should, therefore, in the return on them, reflect that degree of uniqueness that we have in this country, and this return should go primarily to Canadians. It should not be reduced by corporate decision making, or government regulations aimed at serving the public convenience and necessity, for example of consumers in other countries, and notably consumers in the United States.
November 3, 1966

Canada is long on resources, but she is short on such things as money, manpower and markets. This is why we have to specialize and concentrate upon the development of those resources which can be exploited cheaply in terms of men and machines, and why we export many of our materials in a relatively raw state rather than consume them at home.
Our resource industries are essentially our bread and butter industries. They are the industries that can be expected at all times to pay their own way. In fact they pay well, and they should pay well. The average wage is higher than that paid in most other Canadian industries. The take home pay is better and the tax yield is better. This is as it should be, for it is in this resource industry category that Canadians should receive their greatest returns if they are to profit from the exploitation of their natural heritage.
Exports are desirable. Indeed, they are often essential. They help to cut down our engineering and administrative costs. They help to reduce our transportation costs. Lower average costs in Canada can be of great benefit to Canadians as consumers and as manufacturers, and as home owners as well.
Export markets also help us to build larger and more efficient processing plants, plants from which we can also divert our own requirements. Newsprint is a good example; so are our pulp mills, our metal refineries and our fish packing plants.
Processing, however, presents Canadians with a problem. It has been a problem because we would not always sell, or could not always sell, at a profit all of the by-products of our processing plants. With greater industrialization at home, this difficulty is being partially overcome. But we are still faced with discriminatory action on the part of importing countries, and particularly on the part of the United States. The United States, for instance, places a graduated tariff on our exports. The tariff rises with the degree of manufacture or processing of our goods. It rises from zero to 30 per cent or 40 per cent. The more highly processed the goods are, the higher the duty they have to pay when they move across the international boundary line.
The more highly manufactured our exports are, the more highly processed they are, the more man hours they contain per pound, per ton or per cubic foot of product, the more duty they pay entering the United States. This barrier, or sequence of barriers, is designed
Interim Supply
to keep us in the traditional role of a hewer of wood and drawer of water. It is designed to make the United States, and not Canada, the workshop of the North American continent.
Obviously the major objective of any Canadian resource development policy must be to remove and break down these barriers, and to give us access to the larger and more remunerative markets on this continent and throughout the rest of the world.
Freer trade in semi-processed products, therefore, must be our aim. It has been a Canadian objective in the past, but we have not been determined enough about it. With our primary or extractive industries providing fewer jobs and with the prices of primary products tending to decline, further processing must be one of the principal objectives of any Canadian trade policy which has the nation's economic well being at heart.
This brings us to the knotty question of pricing itself. Export prices are not always set as a result of the free interplay of supply and demand. They are not always determined in an impersonal way in the market place. Instead, they are often set as a result of administrative decision making between subsidiary and parent, for example between Canadian branch plant and United States head office.
Big companies which dominate a given field can have things pretty well their own way. Of course, they must cover their costs in Canada, but this is not the same thing as declaring a substantial profit in Canada. There is little to prevent a subsidiary in this country from selling to its United States parent at cost. It covers its costs but declares a minimum profit in this country. Minimum profits mean minimum taxes, and if no shares are sold in the Canadian operation to Canadians then the personal income tax yield, as well as the corporation income tax yield to Canadians, are less than they would be if the Canadian exporter and the United States importer were separate companies.
I do not wish to imply that this is the norm. Pricing at cost is not the general practice between Canadian subsidiaries exporting, and the United States parent companies importing Canadian raw materials into the United States. Nor should I imply that administrative decisions along these lines are necessarily on the increase. But the opportunity is there, and this practice has certainly-existed in the past.

Interim Supply
Canadians would therefore do well to keep asking the Department of National Revenue to investigate what appears on the surface to be unprofitable operations in Canada. The department may then find on closer examination-and I suggest examination in close consultation with expert advisers hi competent technical departments like the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources-that some foreign owned companies may be able to declare higher profits and pay more taxes in Canada.
What constitutes the proper surplus oi profit in Canada is difficult to say. Ideally ar export sale should be made at arms length The seller should sell at the highest price he can get, but the buyer can only buy if the price is right. The latter, that is, the higher price, must be less than any alternative price open to the importer. Of course, these alternatives cannot always be known to us, but as Canadians and as exporters we should always try to charge all that the market will bear.
Normally we could leave this to businessmen, be they employees of foreign owned subsidiaries or not. But a better knowledge of raw material markets and raw material pricing procedures is essential in Canadian government circles if we are to profit from resource development in this country. In other words, federal officials, who are technically competent, officials with a knowledge of industry, and officials with a knowledge of markets and market opportunities, should be taking a closer look at export prices, especially where long term contracts and captive Canadian operations are concerned.
For example, Mr. Chairman, let us consider the National Energy Board, electricity and natural gas. The sale of these commodities is regulated because they are essential goods and because the utilities which sell them are essentially monopolistic in character. In the United States they have a term for the service they provide. There the power utilities and gas companies must build their lines and price their products in such a way as to serve "the public convenience and necessity". This means, among other things, that they must price their products at cost plus a modest or reasonable rate of return, only sufficient to raise the necessary capital but no more. Certainly the profits should not be exceptional, no more than average or sufficient to keep the power moving and the gas flowing.
Unfortunately for Canada as an exporting nation, this idea of minimizing profits has spread across the international boundary line.

It is applied to export sales as well as to domestic consumption. It is applied to Canadian operations even when they are selling all of their output to the United States. One may ask why? The answer is because this is the way that the regulatory authorities direct the power and gas utilities to do things in the United States. There, government intervention is justified on the grounds that it protects the interest of the consumer. The United States consumer is king. All of the activities of the producer and the transporter must be regulated with this end in view.
The Canadian consumer should be protected from monopolistic practices and exceptional profits in much the same way, but the same type of thinking should not be allowed to prevail so far as exports are concerned. Canadians engaged in exporting electricity and natural gas should charge all that the market will bear. They should not charge prices which merely reflect costs, or costs plus a minimum reasonable rate of return, so-called.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
They must charge what the resource really is worth. To price our exports at cost and not charge what the market will bear is to act as if the border does not exist. It means adopting a continental approach to resource development. It is to act as if every Canadian resource belongs to Americans as well as Canadians. It is to abandon the unique position which we should enjoy in this connection. It is to adopt the relatively spineless philosophy of share and share alike. It is to share our Canadian resources with the United States when the United States is not prepared to share its market for certain semi and highly processed goods with us.
Canadians have a bargaining position to maintain, I submit. The uniqueness of our resources should be reflected in our export prices. We must more than cover our costs, and we must have access to United States markets for by-products and up-graded or highly manufactured materials. Then, and only' then, will we be able to develop our resources in a manner which involves the employment opportunities that Canadian industries should generate.
No precise formula, no simple criteria, will fit every case. But, whether it be water which we may never export at all, or whether it applies to commodities which we should like to export in greater quantities such as apples or wheat, a few general principles still might be laid down. These principles should always
November 3, 1966

be observed. They represent the minimum conditions for export. An export proposal which meets these general conditions might then be said to be in the national interest.
The first condition is that Canada must assess its own requirements not only for five, 10 or 25 years ahead, but sometimes for many decades to come. Second, Canada should earmark for export only that amount of the resource which is clearly surplus to the nation's ultimate national, regional and local requirements.
Third, Canada should charge the foreign importing firm or agency a price for the resource which is not only in excess of its cost of supply but which also bears a close relationship to the cost which the importing firm or agency would otherwise have had to pay had it had to rely exclusively on its own requirements or go elsewhere for a source of supply.
Fourth, Canada should never enter into an international contract which results in a lower delivered price for the resource to the importing area as compared to the delivered price of the same resource in adjoining areas in this country. In other words, there always should be a price advantage to the Canadian consumer on the Canadian side. The fifth condition is that Canada must provide for or envisage the eventual repatriation to Canada of these export flows.
Now, I should like to run briefly over the latest Trans-Canada Pipe Line agreement. Canada has assessed its own requirement. Our National Energy Board has decided that Canada already has a supply of natural gas, at least a 25 year supply, to look after our foreseeable Canadian requirements. A surplus, in fact, is deemed to exist. Canada has earmarked for export that amount, which is surplus to our 25 year national, regional and local requirement. This is being done with a cushion left so that if there are errors in our forecasts we are still well covered insofar as our future requirements are concerned, so that that which is exported is readily managed within the sum total of our available supplies.
Canada should charge the foreign importing firm or agency a price which reflects all that the traffic will bear. In reading the report of the National Energy Board it is their opinion, and it is the opinion in the evidence submitted by the interveners that the price charged for western Canadian gas to be exported by the Great Lakes pipe line is competitive. This is their opinion and there
Interim, Supply
is no expert opinion to the contrary. I should underline the fact that we need more information. We need always to be sure that we are charging a competitive price and are not letting the resource go for less than the importer will pay.
Finally, Canada never should enter into an international contract or agreement at a lower delivered price for the resource to the importing firm or agency in one area as compared to the delivered price for the same resource in an adjoining area in Canada. As I understand it there will be a price advantage to Canadians north of the great lakes as opposed to purchases south of the great lakes. My understanding is that the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines rate schedules always have been such that the border prices are higher than the prices charged to a utility in Canada nearby. This applies in Manitoba, the Winnipeg delivered price being lower than it is at Emerson where Canadian gas is exported to the United States.
We have had situations in this country, which now happily are coming to an end, where the delivered price in Canada has been higher than the border price. We have had for a period of some years situations where it has been possible for United States consumers of Canadian gas to get natural gas at prices lower than those charged to Canadians just over the border on our side of the line.
In passing I should like to refer to a statement made recently by the chairman of Westcoast Transmission Company, Mr. Frank McMahon. In the Vancouver Sun of October 13, 1966 he is reported as saying that West-coast-referring to the gas pipe line which runs from northern British Columbia down across that province and out near Vancouver into the Seattle, Portland, Spokane area-as a company never made a reasonable rate of return. He also goes on to say that the wellhead prices back in the Peace River area of British Columbia were also depressed. There is a long history to this.
Essentially United States gas was given first priority in the Pacific north west by the United States authorities. The Canadian pipe line company, in order to get into that market at all, to serve British Columbia consumers, had to accept a price of 22 cents per 1,000 cubic feet at the international boundary line, a few miles from Vancouver. For a few years at Huntingdon the price was 22 cents and the price to the distributor in British Columbia
November 3, 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion was 32 cents per 1,000 cubic feet. This was an anomalous situation. To a degree this situation still obtains. We must not allow decisions of a regulatory body in the United States- decisions dictated by a concern to protect the public convenience and the necessity of consumers in the United States-to strike back at Canadian interests by depressing wellhead prices and the profitability of a pipe line in Canada. Certainly it reduces the incentive to look for gas in the more northern parts of this country.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I called it six o'clock I was talking about our problems of exporting raw materials, and more particularly about our receiving an adequate return for those raw materials. This applies to natural gas because we have not done as well in regard to natural gas, on the west coast at least, as we might have done.
We have had in this country, and I think quite properly, a policy in respect of natural gas to the effect that we must look after Canadian requirements first, and Canadian requirements, in large part at least, are the requirements of southern Ontario and Quebec. In other words, our major markets for energy are in the central provinces.
One of our great problems is the distance from our principal and lowest cost sources of supply of energy to these major markets. When the trans-Canada gas pipe line was built it was by far the longest natural gas pipe line in the world, and it still is. It was then roughly twice the length of the longest line in the world and is still by far the longest anywhere on the face of the globe. This distance is spanned by an efficient pipe line which is now being looped. But it is spanned because, among other things, a lower well-head price is being accepted for natural gas than could be charged for this commodity in British Columbia, Alberta, and to a lesser extent in Saskatchewan, had similar quantities of the gas been permitted to flow southward down the west coast of the United States as far as California and into the United States middle west.
Certainly the oil and gas industries in western Canada, the provinces dependent upon the revenues derived from those industries, and those employed by them, have been affected by our national policy, which I think has been the right one. But when we are looking at alternative routes for bringing gas
2,000	to 2,500 miles from western Canada to Toronto and Montreal, I think we must also look at the economics of transportation. The cheapest and most efficient route is obviously the one to be preferred. It is to be preferred at least to the extent that it will allow the producer in the field to maximize his return
Interim Supply
and at the other end to minimize the cost of energy, in this case natural gas, to the consumer. These factors have to be borne in mind and weighed in the context that we want to keep our major transportation facilities, in so far as possible, under Canadian jurisdiction and under Canadian control.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
Now I should like to deal very briefly with the pamphlet which was distributed to many hon. members by the Canadian Lakehead Industrial Commission. They outlined the arguments in favour of international routing of the new Trans-Canada line and the arguments against it. On the second page we find the advantages of a line south of the great lakes listed as follows: First, construction costs would be lower, resulting in lower delivered prices of gas in southern Ontario. The lower delivered prices are reflected in the fact that the contracts with the distributors are between three to four cents lower than these distributing companies would have to pay to Trans-Canada had it followed the all Canadian route. This is the evidence which those distributing companies presented to the National Energy Board.
The second advantage is that it would be possible to complete the entire project more rapidly. I do not think this is contested in view of the fact that Trans-Canada has completed much of the engineering and has much of its steel already ordered. The third advantage is that the export of natural gas to the United States would be facilitated. Clearly a line which runs south of the great lakes is more directly accessible to the major markets in the United States middle west. The transportation distance from the fields in Alberta is shorter, the cost of movement is lower and the export prices are better. Fourth, financing would be easier. I think it is easier partly because of lower interest rates in the United States. Fifth, Trans-Canada had given a firm contractual commitment to start looping its 30-inch line north of the lakes by 1970. Sixth, there would be safety and protection of continuous service by building another line, this time an international line, to eastern Canada.
I should like to add two additional advantages: One is that the international route passes through and is more directly connected with the major storage fields in Michigan and southern Ontario, and this is an economic advantage and a definite operational advantage, to the trans-Canada pipe line system and to consumers at the eastern end of the

November 3, 1966
Interim Supply
line. The other is that the international line would serve Sault Ste. Marie. In other words, the industries of that area as well as the home owners in Sault Ste. Marie would have natural gas. They would not have this benefit had the line north of the lakes merely been looped.
In all fairness I should also list the disadvantages of the United States route as enumerated by the Canadian Lakehead Industrial Commission. The first disadvantage, and I think it is a significant one, is that the initial economic loss to Canada of the expenditure on wages and materials which would have gone into the looping of an all-Canadian line, now to be spent on the line south of the great lakes and, let us assume, principally in the form of purchases from U.S. steel mills, would be enormous. I think this downgrades the impact of a more economic route on the search for gas in western Canada and the results of somewhat cheaper fuel in eastern Canada. This is the way better economics usually shows up, not in terms of greater capital outlays because greater capital outlays by themselves are no virtue; in fact, they are an indication of wastefulness. What we want is Canadian gas moved to markets in Canada at the lowest possible capital cost, and I suggest that the economics of the international route shows up in this way. It will speed up the search for gas in the west and it will encourage greater industrial development in the east as well as accelerated activity in the whole country.
Second, Canada would lose the economic benefits accruing from operation and maintenance for all time of the international portion of the Trans-Canada line. As anyone who is familiar with modern pipe lines is fully aware, they are highly automated. There is a small operating requirement and maintenance is low. So we are talking about very small sums of money relative to the capital investment involved and relative to the income from the sale of gas at the eastern end of the trans-Canada pipe line. Third, Canada would lose the personal and corporate taxes on construction, operation and maintenance. This is true. Again, however, the better economics of the international line do have compensating effects, both in the west where the gas is fed to the line and in the east in the form of lower prices to consumers. Fourth, Canada would not collect the 50 per cent corporation tax on the major part of the profitable operation lying within the United States. This is

true. Fifth, Canada would not have complete control over a tremendously important but not unlimited resource-natural gas.

speechtext:
I thank the house for permitting me to continue.
In conclusion I wish to answer several questions which have been put to the minister. He has given me his notes and in his absence I will endeavour to reply to those questions on the basis of those notes.
To cover the other two points which are critical of the international routing for the trans-Canada line, the sixth disadvantage is that there would be no assurance of adequate supplies of natural gas for development in this country. Canada is increasingly in the position of a supplier of natural gas not only to its own markets but also to the United States. It is in a strong position to control not only the conditions but also the quantities flowing out of the country. I cannot conceive of the United States, through an agency like the United States Federal Power Commission or in any other way, interrupting flows, endeavouring to frustrate a development of this type, thereby jeopardizing other situations in which it is the importing country and in which the United States owns the industry which is heavily dependent on Canada as its main source of supply.
Would the F.P.C. have the power to set the rates for Canadian gas sold in the United States and could those rates be lower than the rates in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I think the National Energy Board of Canada has the last word. It controls the export permit, it controls the price
November 3, 1966

at which natural gas leaves Canada and, subject to complaints being registered by the consumers in Canada, it also has the power to set import prices. Therefore it really controls prices at both ends of this international loop; in other words, it can dictate the terms. I realize that the United States Federal Power Commission has certain regulatory powers that apply to corporate operations in the U.S. But it cannot override the export price from Canada or the price at which this gas is allowed back into Canada at the eastern end of the line.
I would now like to answer briefly several questions asked by hon. members. The first one appears on page 9386 of Hansard. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked a question concerning transmission costs. The National Energy Board in its report of August, 1966, page 5-34, estimated that there would be an average saving in the cost of transmission via the Great Lakes or international route compared with the northern Ontario or all-Canadian route of 1.7 cents per
1,000	cubic feet over the first five years, and an average of 0.3 cents per 1,000 cubic feet over ten years.
On page 9386 of Hansard the minister, in referring to the saving of 3 cents per 1,000 cubic feet, was referring to the contract which has been signed between Trans-Canada and the Consumers Gas Company. I believe it is 4 cents between Trans-Canada and Union Natural Gas and 2.5 to 4.2 cents with Quebec Natural Gas. So that the negotiations between the distributors in eastern Canada and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines indicate a saving, at least to the distributors, of between 2.5 and 4.2 cents per 1,000 cubic feet.
On page 9463 of Hansard the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, in questioning the availability of gas to northern Ontario, quoted a statement prepared by the Fort William-Port Arthur and District Labour Council. The council brief quoted the president of Twin City Gas Company Limited as saying: "We are sticking our necks out by saying to some industries that the gas will be there." There is other evidence which tends to contradict this. For example, Mr. E. C. Bovey, the president of Northern and Central Gas Company, which is the parent company of Twin City, stated before the National Energy Board at its hearings, and I am now quoting the transcript;
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
Our concern is one of bringing continuing supplies, abundant supplies of natural gas to the area
Interim Supply
we serve in northern and northwestern Ontario at competitive prices in order to continue the development industrially and otherwise of that area.
We have viewed a number of the alternatives, and we feel the alternative of the line below the Great Lakes, the Great Lakes project, is the one that seems to meet these requirements.
In other words, he seems to be supporting both routes, but in his evidence before the National Energy Board he supported the international route.
As reported at page 9464 of Hansard, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked about the prices charged for northern B.C. gas and Peace River gas in the Vancouver and Seattle market areas. Evidence filed before the National Energy Board recently indicated that the average city gate price over the last three years-this is really the average price resulting from the revenue divided by the number of therms, as distinct from the rate-to B.C. Hydro in the Vancouver area was 31.8 cents in 1965, and to Washington Natural Gas in the Seattle area it was 36.7 cents. These prices are in Canadian funds. I gather that in the last few years there have been several rate increases afforded the distributors in the Pacific northwest area, and that is the main reason for the improved situation in Vancouver vis-a-vis Seattle.
These are the main comments, Mr. Chairman, which I wished to make in answer to questions that had been asked.

Mr. Chairman, I had not at first intended to take part in this debate and I do not propose to deal in any great detail with the two specific matters that have rather dominated the debate so far. I am aware that among my colleagues there are those who are at least as capable as, if not more capable than, I am in connection with discussing the details of the pipe line controversy, and I must confess that my interest in military matters declined rather sharply some 50 years ago when I left the service of His Majesty of that day.
However, in listening to this debate I have been struck with this really interesting fact. Here we have two questions which are being discussed in isolation. With all due deference to the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, I do not think it is good enough to pretend that a debate is not taking place in the country at the present time on the issue of continental-ism v. nationalism. I will agree with him that there may well be some phony aspects to it, that those who oppose what is described as

November 3. 1966
Interim Supply
the continentalist position may ascribe to their opponents purposes that they have not got, or may exaggerate the tendency to merge with the United States. Alternatively, those who are classed as being in the continentalist camp may very well exaggerate the position of those they term nationalists and pretend that those they term nationalists are supporting the idea of autarchy and isolation of the Canadian economy.
We should not have any doubt whatever, Mr. Chairman, that this is an issue which is in the minds of the Canadian people. I would commend to the hon. member for Coast-Capilano that he take a trip to Montreal and go to the phone booths in the C.N.R. station where he will discover what I discovered last week, and I will admit it rather shocked me. I found that on the ends of every telephone book in the booths in the C.N.R. station in Montreal someone had stamped the words, and it was a stamp, "Let's join the U.S.A.". This was stamped on a whole series of books. It was cheering that somebody else had come along with a pencil and vigorously scratched it out, but this underlines to me the fact that this is a question in the minds of the Canadian people.
I do not think that it is possible for us to consider either of the two questions that have dominated this debate except in a wider context. I suggest, for instance, that the question of the unification of the armed forces cannot be intelligently discussed until the Canadian people and the Canadian parliament have been given an opportunity to decide just what sort of role they want Canada to play in the world, because on that decision will depend what sort of armed forces, if any, we will require.
Some of the criticisms that I have heard of the minister would seem to indicate that he may be moving in a direction which I for one would heartily approve of, the direction of cutting down our forces to a well-trained force for service with the United Nations. Personally, I happen to think that that is the only sane and sensible policy to adopt. In those terms, Hellyer himself is the ultimate Blimp. In that connection, I found an amazing thing in my foray into the Defence Department last month: the men in charge now are not old Blimps, they are young Blimps. They are passionate devotees of unification and Blimpishly will hear no other argument. This is made easy for them, because any man who opposes armed forces unification-well, let me quote a man who now is serving in a senior staff job in Defence Headquarters: "If there are indications that you do not support the

minister's views, from a career angle you are finished."
When you think of some of the defence ministers we have had, is this a good precedent to establish? If there is a change of government at the next election and a change of forces policy, will all of today's young Blimps at headquarters be fired and even newer Blimps wheeled into their offices and plugged in? Is this, as a policy, safe for Canada?
That is the end of the article by Scott Young in the Globe and Mail of November 2. It is recommended reading for the Liberal party and especially for the Minister of National Defence because if his ego were punctured and he came down off cloud nine I think the demands and requests of opposition members might be met and we would have the committee on national defence reconvened so that we could hear from witnesses called before it the evidence which they are prepared to give. The minister has assured the house that he will not censor any evidence. The word "censor" has been used, whereas last week we were using the word "tampered". The hon. member for Leeds certainly fouled up that word last night, and possibly from here on we should use the word "censor". In order to avoid the hon. member for Leeds having to look up the meaning of the word-I should like to draw to the attention of members of the Liberal party that there is only one minister on the front benches but this is just what we can expect from that government-he will find the meaning of "censor" as given in the Oxford Dictionary to be:
An official in some countries whose duty it is to inspect all books, journals, dramatic pieces, etc., before publication, to secure that they shall contain nothing immoral, heretical, or offensive to the government.
I presume that the Minister of National Defence will not adopt that attitude and will allow freedom of expression to all witnesses who in the future are called before the national defence committee. The hon. member for Leeds stood up to defend the minister. He denied there was any tampering with the evidence and then contradicted himself by referring later in his remarks to what he called untampered evidence. This was a direct contradiction by that member. The minister himself in recent days denied that our defence forces have not been kept up to their full requirement and then within five minutes of making that statement admitted to very grave shortages in the armed forces personnel.
November 3, 1966



I had been looking for the opportunity to go back into the history of this matter while certain members were in the house but I do not intend to go too far back at this time. However, if the Liberal party wishes to go back into history, why do they go back only two or three years? Why do they not go back and give us a full resume of what went on when members on that side of the house were in a very involved position in respect of defence? They could have taken us back and possibly given us a story about the horses they had on the payroll under the present Minister of Industry. They could have gone back and told us about the stupid position they took in respect of the Bomarc issue. At the time they were taking their position in respect of the Bomarc missiles, the Bomarcs were being phased out in the United States. Yet they claimed they had to fulfil a commitment. One commitment which should be fulfilled is that of loyalty by this minister to the people of this nation so that this nation can be provided with the information which will allow the opposition and the government working together to establish an armed service in this country of which we can be proud rather than a police force which would serve their purposes, whatever they may be.
These purposes were referred to several times by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Here again there is further contradiction, because the Secretary of State for External Affairs today referred to himself as the foreign minister. This is a further indication of the fact that they are destroying completely the national interests of this country not only in matters of defence but in many other aspects of our economy.
There is a duty upon the minister to provide us with the truth. In the last few weeks, through a favourable press, the Liberals have told the people of this country that the member for Edmonton-Strathcona backed away from making a charge. They know that the member for Edmonton-Strathcona put his seat on the line in making the necessary charge. They also are aware of the fact that the Minister of National Defence himself was the only person responsible for that charge not getting the proper hearing.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The member for Leeds the other night said that the member for Edmonton-Strathcona went on a C.B.C. program and made a slanderous charge. The Liberals say he has no courage in this house, but he has proven that he has courage. It is the Minister of National

Defence who has proven himself to be gutless and on more than one score. He has proven himself to be gutless in this house and he continues to do so day after day. He has also proven himself to be gutless outside this house. Every member of parliament has immunity in the house, but they do not enjoy that immunity when they make statements on the C.B.C. If the Minister of National Defence has the guts he says he has why did he not do something about the slanderous remarks he has suggested were made? The Minister of National Defence continues to prove himself gutless.

Mr. Chairman, since the atmosphere is heavy with accusations, in order to lend some variety to the debate, I shall take advantage of the study of those estimates to call the government's attention to another national scandal.
The present case involves the C.N.R. which, in my opinion, has become the worst nest of patronage among all the Canadian companies. When the doubters have an opportunity to do so, I urge them to take a look at the payroll of that company, especially the payroll of senior officials, because the same names always appear among the heads of some divisions, whether in Quebec city, Montreal or Toronto.
And even though that situation has existed for several years, we have yet to be shown that relationship means competence. On the other hand, we have proof that hundreds of young men who, through incapacity or misconduct, have been unable to complete their studies in regular schools, have become students at the expense of the C.N.R. Following their studies, those young men have been appointed inspectors and throughout the country, thousands of workers must submit to every whim of those new inspectors who know nothing. Those workers include the station agent who, all his life, has scrupulously performed the following combined duties: finance agent, telegraph agent, ticket agent, freight agent, express agent. That man is also responsible for keeping the stations clean and in good order.
That agent now works under the orders of those young greenhorns who travel across the country, all expenses paid, as inspectors. Each inspector is supposed to be an expert in one

Interim Supply
field, of course, and they are expert in accounting, in freight, express inspectors, sanitation inspectors; inspectors are to be found everywhere there are workers.
The government is aware of the fact, I suppose, that the overly large number of inspectors working for the C.N.R. was one of the main reasons for the strike last summer. In the same week, six inspectors may visit the same station, half of those inspectors are unscrupulous and submit false reports.
I could name a few of those inspectors and give their addresses. They are supposed to meet the customers of the various services of the C.N.R. such as the freight or the express. Now, they mention in their report the names of persons to whom they ascribe some statements concerning the C.N.R. service and, moreover, the persons mentioned have never been visited by any inspector; therefore, they have never been asked to give their impressions. How much does this dishonest work cost the Canadian taxpayers? I take the liberty of quoting one of my questions in that connection, namely question No. 1,887 which appeared in the order paper:
What was the total amount of expenses claimed through the expense accounts granted by the Canadian National Railways to its non-union employees for the year 1965?
The parliamentary secretary gave the following answer, as reported on page 8334 of Hansard:
The management of Canadian National Railways advises as follows: The company does not differentiate between expenses claimed by union and non-union employees. No record is kept of amounts that may have been paid to non-union employees only.
Do you know of an independent company which could operate regardless of an elementary rule of logic which states that no business, nothing at all can operate without some form of control?
Only a crown corporation can ignore this rule. And under the aegis of the Department of Transport, Canadian National Railways officials allow themselves to pay out without stint.
Under the aegis of the Department of Transport, employees get more expense money than they do wages, starting with the president of the company.
Not only are we unable to get information on expenses, but wages are just as much a

mystery. Another question put on the order paper, Question No. 1,868, reads as follows:
How many employees of the Canadian National Railways earn an annual salary of (a) $4,000 to $6,000 (b) $6,000 to $8,000 (c) $8,000 to $10,000 (d) $10,000 to $15,000 (e) $15,000 to $25,000 (f) over $25,000?
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport replied, as recorded on page 8329:
The management of Canadian National railways advises as follows: It has not been considered in the best interests of the company to disclose data on employees' earnings in the manner requested.
This was not the day for honest and clear answers, since that same day, on the same page, in reply to Question No. 1,869:
How many hours a week must the agent in charge of a station doing $50,000 worth of business a year, work to maintain that standard with (a) C.N.R. (b) C.P.R.?
The Secretary of State's reply, as recorded on page 8329, reads as follows:
In so far as the Department of Transport is concerned :
(a) The management of Canadian National Railways advises as follows: Canadian National station agents work a standard week of forty hours and are paid on a salary basis.-The federal government does not have statistics on the amount of business they do.
The Canadian National Railways, a company which is said to have administrative staff, a company in the hands of a number of handsomely paid people, having at its head a president costing the Canadian people $75,000 a year, over and above expenses, told could be achieved by private enterprise which would operate without method, as in the case of the Canadian National. Whether it is not considered in the best interest of the company to disclose employees' earnings.
The company does not keep track of expenses for which employees claim reimbursement; it does not require statistics to be kept in this regard.
Mr. Chairman, I have not been sitting in the house for very long, but the short time I have been able to spare for research has enabled me to realize that the balance-sheets of this company are all alike, namely they all show a deficit. This is not surprising, under such an administration.
We can hardly imagine the success which could be achieved by private enterprise which would operate without method, as in the case of the Canadian National. Whether it is a business, trucking, construction or industrial enterprise, any manager would require
November 3. 1966

reports: inventories, reports on expenses, and efficiency reports. When one wants profits, one begins by insisting upon an intelligent management.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Hence, when we consider the balance-sheet of the Canadian National, we are concerned with its poor management and we wonder also how it happens that such an intelligent person as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) is forced to defend a company managed so stupidly.
Waste is not limited to inspection; there is waste of human capital inside the company itself. On account of economy, station agents are transferred unconsciously, without any consideration for services rendered.
In a letter he wrote me recently, an agent told me that after 45 years of service, 45 years of work in an important station, he was transferred 500 miles from his family to perform night work, and that on account of economy.
And also on account of economy, the Canadian National is taking steps to close several stations throughout Canada. How can we talk about savings when figures regarding the amount of business of those stations do not even exist?
The proof that those figures do not exist is that agents with a yearly turnover of only $50,000 will keep their position, while others with a yearly turnover of $150,000 have been informed to clear out and to gather all their books, because those books will be taken to a central office.
The fate of the railway workers has nothing to be envied either, because with the way the C.N.R. is extending the sections, always on account of economy, their number is decreasing from day to day. And the less there are honest workers who, through their work, maintain the railways, the more there are supervisors. It is rather common to see three foremen for two workers. Mr. Chairman, when supervisors have to supervise the supervision office, it is time for a change.
We hope that the Minister of Transport will do everything in his power to rectify that situation and that the house will give him the sympathy he deserves; in fact, in his office, he does deserve our sympathy, because with a mere $27,000 a year, he is responsible before parliament and the Canadian people for the mistakes of a company president who gets a salary three his own.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose it is the sad experience of most backbenchers to have to speak to an empty house, but I think the Liberal party might well have been here in large numbers because I intend to make, if I can, a positive contribution to this debate. This is not a laughing matter; this should not be a Red Skelton program. I believe we are discussing tonight, as we have been for the last two days, the most important subject facing the Canadian people, yes, the northern hemisphere and in fact the whole world, the question of survival. If the Canadian people are not interested in survival, why should any party or any government have the colossal nerve to ask us to spend on defence $1,672 million of our hard earned income.
I do not think we have to spend that amount of money to become an international police force. But if we took a realistic view of the situation it might be that we should spend a great deal more money, after looking at the jungle world in which we live and the forces of evil with which we have to contend. I gave seven years of my young life to war, and I do not want to repeat that experience any more than does anybody else in this country. But I would go to war again if the dignity of man were to be dragged through the dirt. As one hon. member said tonight, we should all be willing to take this attitude.
Sometimes I am half ashamed of my country and half ashamed of this institution when a junior member like myself has to lecture this house. But I am afraid that if I kept silent the rocks of Canada from Newfoundland to Vancouver Island would speak because it is time somebody stood up here and spoke from their guts, and I am not worried about whether I have any.
In the world of today we cannot ignore the nuclear role. When the nuclear policy of this country was discussed some years ago I for one had no fuzzy thinking. I knew what faced Hon. Howard Green in those days as chairman of the anti-nuclear committee. I also knew the problem which faced the hon. member for Calgary North who was at that time minister of national defence. If I may say so, when some of the dust has settled we might well look back to the days of the leadership of the hon. member for Calgary North in respect of defence and admire at least his forthrightness and clear thinking on defence policies.

Hear, hear.

November 3, 1966
Interim Supply

We should admire these qualities even if the hon. member could not see as clearly as Hon. Howard Green the necessity for a very deep and sincere wish that men gather around the council tables of the world and outlaw the horror which ruined my young life in its most important seven years.
I believe in the defence of this hemisphere. I also believe in the complete support of our North American allies. But I am not one of those who want this at the price of our sovereignty. I know the problem that exists in the United States. The Americans have only one friend amongst the armed nations of the world-little old Canada. Can they rely on de Gaulle in another war? Can they rely on Mr. Wilson's England? Churchill has gone. That great voice of freedom has been stilled forever. I remember standing in an old pub in England and listening to Mr. Churchill saying, "We will fight on the beaches." We were on the beaches, and I can tell you that we did not have very much more than the rocks at Brighton to fight with. When that great man spoke from his guts, and that is what he had, there was very little else to fight with, and the whole western world was inspired.
I did not think that in one generation the western peoples would descend into the pit of defeatism where they would say: There is nothing left for us to do but be bird-watchers or policemen on the Gaza strip. I too am proud of our armed forces and I believe in integration of a sort. Are combined operations a new thing? Did Corporal Hellyer invent integration? I saw integration in practice. Thousands of my pals died at Dieppe. I wish I had been at Dieppe with them.
Is unification something new? The Spartans knew something about unification. Three hundred men stood at Thermopylae: You did not have to preach to them about unification or about a united effort for the case of Greece. Does the Minister of National Defence expect me to be something less, or does he expect those of us who have lived in the days of Churchill, Lord Alexander and General Montgomery to be something less? I am sure that General Montgomery and Lord Alexander would be only too pleased to appear before a defence committee anywhere in the western world to give their views about integration and unification. They would be the last two men alive to say that the western world can afford to be pacifist. I say without hesitation, would to God we could be. I would

like to see the day when we can spend our $1J billion of defence money on feeding the hungry people of the world instead of buying expensive military hardware. Because we are no longer the government, are we to sit in silence while the same people who said we had no right to cancel the expensive Arrow program now want us to be bird watchers? What good will it do to be watchers of this kind?
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I said before that I believe in helping our American allies protect perhaps the last citadel of freedom, the North American continent. If we cannot keep this place safe and free, if we cannot be strong and hold power in the world, how can we afford to be generous abroad? I think that the enemies of the United States are often the enemies of freedom. Are we to follow their advice on what to do when they say "Yankee go home"? Where did that phrase come from? Where does the phrase "Get out of Viet Nam" come from? I do not hear very much of that coming from Australia, I do not hear very much of that coming from New Zealand, and I do not hear too much of it coming from the senior member of the Commonwealths lusty children.
If the old lion is tired, what are we going to do about it? There is the peace-keeping role. Every man in this room knows it would be no good sending our men to Cyprus or to the Gaza Strip if it were not for the powerful, alert, well armed and willing to fight neighbour to our south. Defence is too hot to handle and so we play around with our little Red Skelton programs, dragging each other through the mud. Just keep it up and you will see what our friends to the left, who have never taken a realistic view of the defence of freedom as we know it, will say. They would like to take over, and then it will be too late.
If this government has a consistent defence policy, I would like to see them bring it before us. Why is this the first opportunity we have had to stand up and say what we think should be done? The question of national service has been too hot to handle ever since 1917. We got around it in world war two. We relied on volunteers. I wonder whether we have the right to rely on volunteers. I wonder whether a man has the right to involve his country in a war when the consensus in the country is not behind that war. Do we need leadership in defence? I do not think it is right to wait for public opinion to push us.
November 3, 1966

If Churchill had waited for public opinion to push him, he would never have been where he was when we needed him. He stood practically alone, and because he told his countrymen things they did not want to hear he had to wait until he was an old man before he was given the opportunity to show he was right. For instance, Eden was right when the little ships put the Graf Spee to shame. It is not enough to believe in freedom. Somebody has to do something about it.
I am one of those who do not think we can keep Canadian sovereignty and keep from being completely absorbed by the great republic to the south unless we are willing to pay our way. I said in this house and I say again that I think we should pay our way and take the first moral, brave and spiritual step of admitting that the price of freedom cannot come too high in money or in men. It may well be that the policy of raising an adequate armed force can be achieved through a voluntary system. I would like to think it could. However, if it cannot I would not hesitate, as does the minister of defence, to call upon the Canadian people to take a really good look at the question of survival.
We should consider how far we are willing to go to fight for our own freedom and independence and, I would not hesitate to say, for our national honour because I am one who thinks that Canada's national honour is not dead. As far as I can see, it is in a deep slumber and its snoring comes to us mainly from the treasury benches.
The question of unification and integration is not the only one about which we should be worried. There are many other aspects of our national defence which need a great deal of consideration. What are we going to do about military hardware? I was greatly pleased to hear that our striking power in antisubmarine warfare is greater today than it has ever been and that by some necromancy we are going to be able to do this with fewer ships and fewer men. I believe this is possible but I think it is quite irrelevant if we have no intention of ever involving ourselves in antisubmarine warfare now or at any other time. I suppose the Minister of National Defence knows how many nuclear submarines there are in the world today. I do not, but I know they are there. If we have this super-submarine striking power, where is it?
I think that our committee system has been good and we have expanded it, but what in the world is the good of a defence committee which is muzzled? Surely the Minister of 23033-603
Interim Supply
National Defence has some confidence in the views of serving soldiers, airmen and sailors. If he has not, then somebody must be seriously wrong. Either he is wrong or the men that he is calling are wrong. Anybody who has ever served in the army knows perfectly well that when a man has a good, superior officer he need not hesitate to take his advice. Before any attack our colonel always held a meeting and he asked each and every officer in his command to criticize the plan fully. We knew that at zero hour we had to go ahead and do what we were told but, as I say, any officer for whom we had the slightest respect never hesitated to pick the brains of lesser men.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Who is this straw man, this bogeyman of brass, who is bullying the defence minister? Where is he? How is he doing this? The hon. member for Leeds asks: How do you tamper with an admiral? I might ask another question: How does a serving admiral hope to bully the defence minister? Surely he can say anything he likes. Does the defence minister say that any serving member of any one of the three forces, or a member of the proposed unified forces, could hope to influence him against his own conscience and will? If that is the case, then we certainly need a new defence minister. We can afford to have officers who do not know all the answers but we cannot afford a defence minister who will not listen to the experts in the various commands.
We have these experts, and let hon. members opposite not raise this straw man again and say that the Tories have no faith in them. We have a great deal of faith in our defence experts. Day by day we are going to keep hammering at this question until we have hammered out a sensible defence policy. We have been asked half a dozen times today what we think about defence policy, but the government does not want to hear our answer.
I am going to tell you what I think about it, Mr. Chairman. I may be wrong but as one member out of 265 I have the right to state what I think is the cross-section of opinion of this country. The cross-section of public opinion in this country must be that we should all stand to defend Canada to a man. There is unification there from one end of Canada to the other. Loyalty to Canada is not a party matter. There is no monopoly of patriotism.

I know the war records of many of the members of this house on both sides, and I think we should have had a full-fledged debate on this subject a long time ago. It is not enough to say that we have a defence committee which can do this. We cannot all be members of that committee. The reason we have a committee of limited size is to enable 15 or 20 members to thrash out some of these problems. But this cannot be done unless there is reliance placed upon the witnesses who appear before you.
I do not think that a government with a defence policy worthy of the name should be afraid to have the frankest expression of opinion of every serving member of the armed forces. Having been a service officer myself I cannot imagine that I would do or say anything designed to weaken our strength or to weaken a strong, effective government defence policy. But as a private soldier, let alone as a serving general or admiral or air vice marshal, it would certainly be criminal negligence if I were not willing to come forward and stand up to any type of badgery.
Are hon. members opposite indicating that we have officers in the armed forces who would rather collect their pensions than have a safe Canada? If such there be, I say to the government that they should put them out of the armed forces now and replace them with somebody who has the proper kind of integrity and courage. We can face up to the truth. If we have run into dead ends in our defence policy over the last 20, 40 or 100 years it is no good crying over spilled milk. We must decide what we are going to do now and where we go from here.
I suggest that we had better get a longterm defence policy which seeks to keep Canada strong and free as long as she is a nation. We will always need men, and unless I am vastly mistaken the spot wars which have broken out all over the world recently and are still raging in many places are a threat to us all, our homes, ideals and principles. Wishful thinking can spread like a disease to cripple a whole nation.
I said before and I want to say again that I am not a defeatist. I do not think we have yet got to the point of no return. If I may speak for my colleagues, there is not a member of the official opposition who is not willing to go the whole way. We are willing to listen and to talk. We only want a chance to be heard and we only want a chance to hear. We want to hear from those who can give us the best information.

We in the armed forces served under such men as General Guy Simonds in the Canadian army. Let him appear before the committee. I think he knows something about combined operations, call it integration if you like. I think Lord Louis Mountbatten would be very pleased to make a tour of Canada and visit every defence post. He would be above suspicion of being mixed up in our local politics. He would not worry whether we used what he said during the next general election campaign. Let us hear him and at least learn some of the lessons the British learned on the question of integration.
If you will forgive me for a moment, Mr. Chairman, I will put a little sentiment into this speech. The Black Watch regiment happens to wear my family tartan. I think that some of these points which mean nothing to those who have not worn the Black Watch tartan might well bear consideration, even in this twentieth century when these sort of things are not supposed to count. Perhaps hon. members may think it makes no difference to a guards officer that his buttons are two up, two down on the front of his jacket. Perhaps they might think that the two swaths which are cut out of the gaiters worn by members of the Black Watch do not mean anything. I would remind them that this means that in their centuries of service to their king and country only twice in 500 years did they give ground. There does come a time in anybody's military service when there is no place to go, and if you give ground, you give all. This is the tradition of the Black Watch.
I do not want to labour this point, but there is not a regiment serving Canada which was ever called to its colours that did not have some idea of the sanctity of tradition. Nations that forget their history very soon have no history. This is the thing that makes a good man great. It makes a soldier fight when there should not be any fight left in him. This is the kind of stuff that we want to hear, and I think we need to hear it today more than at any other time.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
We know that this unification program, this integration program, cannot be brought in overnight, right though it may be. We have time. Why should it be necessary for any one man or small group of men, no matter how right they think they are, to deny the right to express an opinion to those who may differ from them in some degree? I should think
November 3, 1966

that any government which only polled one-third of the popular vote in the country, and which had any feeling for its duty, would want to know what the rest of the country felt. Even though I do not deny them the right to be bold, to be imaginative, to be out in front, to be leaders and to give us a dynamic defence policy which we had not dreamed of, I still believe there is room for the opinions of others to be heard. But I do not think all the members on this side of the house are dreaming. I think we are facing reality in this jungle world of the 20th century. When we are ready, when the race of man has matured and we are prepared to furl the battle flags forever in the parliament of man, even then it may be found that we on this side of the house are willing to co-operate in the great march toward peace which is so desired.
Is it traitorous to criticize something which we believe to be wrong? Am I partisan because I say we should give our serving officer the right to contribute in every way, not only with their muscles and their guns but with their imagination, their courage and their right to speak freely? The strongest armies in the world have always been those armies which have believed in the people. The army of the French revolution at its best was an army of the people. Nothing could stop it. With staves and brickbats and scythes they tore down the Bastille. However, they forgot their aims. They went out on imperialistic forays.

Mr. Chairman, such is the "cabbages and kings" nature of the discussion we have been having on this interim supply motion that we have been able to talk today about pipe lines, admirals and level crossings. Another item we can talk about concerns northern affairs and it is my hope to put a few observations on record in this regard.
We have heard a good deal in the last few days about the fruits of integration. I suggest seriously that whatever value integration may have for the armed services it might well be given a try in the area of northern affairs. I was one of the members of the committee on northern affairs who visited the Arctic and the Northwest Territories this summer. We saw an area there which is about half the size of the United States and 23033-603J
Business of the House
carries a population equal to that of a good sized city, between 40,000 and 50,000. The bases we visited there are for the most part administrative outposts in which 2,000 or
3,000	people at the most are living. They are usually civil servants. It is no criticism of them to say that they spend a large part of their time looking after one another. Of course, they are also concerned with looking after and helping the native people in the areas in which they are located.
What struck me about the efforts being made in these administrative outposts was the fact that in the communities one found so many different departments of government at work-Northern Affairs, Transport, Justice, Health and Welfare, and, of course, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. My feeling was, and it remains with me, that we could do a better job in some of these areas if we set up an integrated service or a unified service under which, instead of this variety of services under different headings, we could carry out a unified operation. I believe better results would more quickly be obtained at less expense if there were an integrated task force to deal with the problems of the north.
I should like to say something about education. There is a great need for a stepped-up program, particularly of adult education. In some northern areas we found a situation where natives who had been living all their lives until recently in tents or igloos are now learning to live in houses while their children go to schools and try to assimilate the knowledge taught to children in the south. A great deal of progress has been made in the north in the field of education but more remains to be done, particularly with regard to adult education. May I call it ten o'clock?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: ABOLITION OF MEANS TEST IN PROPOSED PENSION INCREASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, October 26, as recorded in Hansard at page 9126, I put this question to the Prime Minister:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the sharp criticism of a means test which we heard from the government side last night, will the government make sure that there is no means test attached to the proposed increase in the old age pension?
My reference to sharp criticism was to a speech that had been made the previous night by the Minister of National Health and Welfare during debate on second reading of the medicare bill. During the course of his speech the minister criticized the "medicare for the needy plan" proposed by the Progressive Conservatives on the grounds that it was a means test, something to which the Liberals were opposed.
The Prime Minister's reply to my question of last Wednesday was:
Mr. Speaker, I have to ask my hon. friend to wait until the introduction of the legislation when these matters will all be made clear.
I then posed a supplementary question as follows:
In view of the fact that the government has given itself additional time to draft this legislation, will it not reconsider its position regarding the means test?
There was no answer to my supplementary question so I gave notice that I wished to raise it during one of these adjournment debates. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, I rise again at this time to make as strong an appeal as I can to the government to desist from the idea of attaching a means test in any form to the proposed increase for the old age pensioners. It will not get away with an attempt to say that any kind of a test that it may be devising is not a means test.
I remind the government that the original Old Age Pensions Act that came into effect in 1927 had in it what was popularly known as a means test. It was popularly known as that, but it was the most unpopular provision we had on the statute books at that time, and


eventually we got rid of it. Officially it was an income test, and the same is true for the means test in the war veterans allowance legislation and any other legislation. None of these tests is called a means test. It is always called by some more euphonious name, but when you require people to submit information as to their other income before they get a benefit, you are submitting those people to a means test.
I submit that the government will not get away with this play on words with respect to this matter. I remind the government that recently a Gallup poll was taken on this question, and those who were polled regarding their opinion about a means test on old age pensions were 54 per cent in favour of no means test, and 40 per cent in favour of a pension being paid after a means test. In addition there were 6 per cent who were undecided. That means that of those who expressed an opinion, about 57 per cent were against the means test, and only 43 per cent were willing to consider it. I suggest that this is an overwhelming figure on this important issue.
Currently there are rumours as to variations the government may make in its means test, whether the first $30 other income will disqualify a person or whether there will be some 50-50 proposition, but I say to the government that any of these devices will bring down a storm of criticism upon its head.
I freely give to the government this piece of friendly advice: do not again make the kind of mistake you made in the field of old age pensions that you made in 1957. You thought then you would get away with a $6 increase on what was then a $40 pension and as a result you lost the 1957 election.
I submit that with all the progress we have made in this country in getting rid of the means test, if this government puts it back on even a portion of the old age pension it will be the worst political mistake the Liberals have made since 1957. I am not concerned, of course, about political mistakes on the part of the Liberals, but I am concerned about what it does to the respect and dignity of our older people. Do not tell us that we are not with the new ideas about guaranteed annual income-the language the government wants to use. All the government is doing is using high-sounding words to cover up the iniquity of something as old as the hills. Call it what you may; if you force people to tell what

they have in other income before they get this increase, then it is a means test. Do not say there is no means test if you force people to report their income in order to get the pension increase. Not only will it be unpopular with our people but it will be a blow to the self-respect and dignity of our older people. So I urge that the government do what I have been appealing to it to do every time I have brought up this question, namely, to reconsider its position with regard to the means test.
It now seems fairly clearly established that the government is going to do something at this session regarding aid to the old age pensioners. I plead with the government to stick with the principle and the policy accepted in 1950 and 1951, and brought into effect in 1952, namely, that our old age security pension be paid to all our older people without a means test of any kind. The pension must be raised, but let it be a pension as of right, across the board, to all our older people.

PENITENTIARIES-REPORTED CHARGES AGAINST ADMINISTRATION OF WOMEN'S PRISON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I attempted to put a question to the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) with regard to statements issued by the former superintendent, the former psychologist and the former social worker at the women's prison at Kingston. In my opinion these statements contained the most serious charges, in respect of a change of policy which probably have ever been made against our correctional system in the last 15 or 20 years. I rise tonight because my question was ruled out of order. In a matter of such importance I think the Solicitor General should welcome the opportunity to make a statement and explain as soon as possible what is going on.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The people of Canada have been increasingly concerned with the problems of crime, criminals and correctional services for a good many years. This is not surprising in view of the fact that Canada has two and a half times as many people, when one adjusts for population differences, in our prisons and jails as have countries such as Great Britain. Since the Archambault report of 1938 and particularly since 1956 when Mr. Justice Fauteux and his committee reported, we have been advised to turn from the punitive methods we have always used to more modern and humane methods of treatment of prisoners. The Ouimet committee undoubtedly will make the same recommendations.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
While all this has been going on and while the best medical, legal and social service leaders in the country who have been studying our correctional system have been making such recommendations, the commissioner of penitentiaries has been turning the clock back to a system of repression, punishment and discipline. In a couple of weeks, according to the Solicitor General, the committee headed by Mr. Justice Ouimet will report on the maximum security unit built in Montreal. This unit was built against the advice of all professionals in this field. It was completed in 1966 and is much like prisons of the middle ages, without windows for the prisoners. I presume it was built on the advice of the commissioner of penitentiaries and the psychiatrist at Kingston, whose advice I suggest has been wrong on every occasion. Surely that unit will be condemned by the Ouimet commission. We will then be saddled with an institution which has cost millions but is obsolete.
This condition attains so far as the women's prison at Kingston is concerned. The superintendent, the psychologist and another worker of the former staff have recently suggested that the department has changed its policy in respect of the rehabilitation of inmates to one of discipline. The commissioner of penitentiaries says that there has been no change. The acting warden apparently believes in the same kind of discipline in women's institutions as in men's institutions.
The views expressed by the former members of this staff have been endorsed by the Elizabeth Fry Society of Ontario and a brief to this effect was submitted to the minister. I am sorry to say that one cannot expect much
Novembei 3, 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion change in the present attitude of the commissioner of penitentiaries regarding the administrative policies at the women's institution. This is true in spite of the fact the number of prisoners who return was cut from seven out of ten to three and a half out of ten. Since 1965 there has been a considerable and steady change from that type of rehabilitative treatment of inmates to a disciplinary treatment of a kind which we do not see in correctional systems anywhere else in the world.
The Solicitor General as the head of this system ought to know what is taking place and whether or not this kind of disciplinary action is taking place. If it is he should make *changes. As I suggested privately to the minister, perhaps this is the time to ask for the resignation of the commissioner of penitentiaries because his views are no longer consistent with the desires of the Canadian people.
The orders in respect of prisoners in the women's institution were revised in June of this year. Discipline has been imposed and many of these prisoners have been kept under constant surveillance. The acting warden has been quoted in newspapers as having said that he believes women inmates should be disciplined in the same manner as men. I wonder whether the acting warden has ever heard of the Archambault and Fauteux reports and their recommendations.
Sometimes I wonder whether the facts I have given are accepted. If anyone thinks they should not be I should like to refer them to a list of questions submitted to the Solicitor General by the Elizabeth Fry Society. These are questions that I presume the minister has not answered yet. I should like to read some of these questions into the record and I suggest the answers should be obvious. These questions surely would not arise if our penal system so far as women are concerned did not create difficulties.
The questions I should like to read are:
When Is solitary confinement used?
How long can inmates be held in solitary confinement?
Is there a limit on the number of days in a month or a year that an inmate can be held in solitary confinement?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always welcome the interventions of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. [Mr. Orlikow.l
Orlikow) because although he is critical of the minister I know he also has a genuine interest in the inmates of our correctional institutions. He is one of the few members in the house who, it seems to me, manifests a genuine interest in this regard. However, I cannot accept his views in their entirety. I would say to him that I have not only read the brief of the Elizabeth Fry Society but I have had the benefit of two meetings with the former superintendent of the prison for women at Kingston and also interviews with two of the former employees. In addition, I have made two extensive visits to the prison this year.
I must say that whenever there is a difference of opinion in these matters I have found there is a great deal to be said on both sides of the question. I think it is only fair to say that, I accept responsibility and at the urging of the commissioner the government set up a special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons to examine the physical plant of the prison and see what is going on there. In addition, the government set up the Canadian committee on corrections under Mr. Justice Ouimet to study in depth the training and treatment best suited to the inmates of our institutions. I told the house, I believe in answer to a question put by the hon. member, that a number of the recommendations of the Fauteux commission had been implemented; I believe they total 30.
We realize that this is a tremendous task. It is a very difficult and complicated one. I have no illusions about the problem of recidivism but I believe we are making some progress in this direction, I hope shortly to be able to publish figures of the number of inmates in our institutions compared with the number several years ago. I believe these figures will be encouraging in the sense that it is a declining number. However, you cannot always depend upon numbers in these matters because for some unknown reason the balance shifts from time to time.
